sections.body:
Julia has two ways to turn a value into text:

* `print` (and `println`, `string`, `"$x"`) writes the value **for humans**:
  a string without its quotes, a character without its single quotes.
* `show` (and `repr`) writes it **as Julia would read it back**: quotes,
  escapes, type information where needed. This is what you see in the REPL
  and in error messages.

The REPL actually calls `show(io, MIME"text/plain"(), x)`, a richer,
possibly multi-line form; `repr(x)` and `show(x)` use the compact one-line
form. Notice the differences in the output below: `print` loses the
information that `"hi"` was a string and `:sym` a symbol, `repr` keeps it.

examples.code:
x = "hi"
print(x); println()
show(x); println()
println(string(x), "  ", repr(x))
println(string('c'), "  ", repr('c'))
println(string(:sym), "  ", repr(:sym))
println("tab\there", "  ", repr("tab\there"))
examples.output:
hi
"hi"
hi  "hi"
c  'c'
sym  :sym
tab	here  "tab\there"

examples.caption: One value, two `show` forms: compact (inside `println` of a vector, and `repr`) and `text/plain` (what the REPL prints).
examples.code:
v = [1.5, 2.0, 3.25]
println(v)
println(repr(v))
show(stdout, MIME"text/plain"(), v)
println()

examples.caption: Defining `Base.show(io, x)` for your type changes how `print`, `repr`, interpolation and containers display it.
examples.code:
struct Point
    x::Int
    y::Int
end
p = Point(1, 2)
println(p)
Base.show(io::IO, p::Point) = print(io, "(", p.x, ", ", p.y, ")")
println(p, "  ", repr(p), "  ", "at $p")
[p, Point(3, 4)]
examples.output:
Point(1, 2)
(1, 2)  (1, 2)  at (1, 2)
2-element Vector{Point}:
 (1, 2)
 (3, 4)

sections.title: print, show, string and repr

sections.body:
`print` and `write` take an optional first argument: the **stream** to
write to. Besides `stdout` and files, an `IOBuffer` is a stream in memory.
Write pieces into it, then `String(take!(io))` turns the bytes into a
string and empties the buffer.

This is the efficient way to build a long string in a loop. `s *= piece`
copies the whole string every time, so building `n` pieces that way costs
time proportional to `n²` (the `format-number-column` problem measures it).

`sprint(f, args...)` is the shortcut: it creates the buffer, calls
`f(io, args...)` and returns the string.

examples.code:
io = IOBuffer()
write(io, "abc")
print(io, 42, ' ', 3.5)
println(io, "!")
s = String(take!(io))
println(repr(s))
println(isempty(take!(io)))
println(sprint(show, "quoted"))
println(sprint(io -> join(io, 1:5, " + ")))
examples.output:
"abc42 3.5!\n"
true
"quoted"
1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5

sections.title: Building text in an IOBuffer

sections.body:
The `Printf` standard library gives C-style formatting: `@printf` prints and
`@sprintf` returns a string. A format spec is `%[flags][width][.precision]type`:

* types: `d` integer, `f` fixed-point, `e` scientific, `g` shortest, `s`
  anything printed with `print`, `x` hexadecimal;
* width pads to at least that many characters, right-aligned; the flag `-`
  aligns left and `0` pads with zeros; `+` always shows the sign;
* `.2f` means two digits after the decimal point (rounded, not truncated).

`@printf(io, ...)` writes to any stream, an `IOBuffer` included. The format
must be a literal string: it is compiled by the macro.

examples.caption: Fixed widths line up columns.
examples.code:
using Printf
for (name, qty, price) in [("apple", 3, 0.5), ("watermelon", 1, 4.25), ("fig", 12, 0.333)]
    @printf("%-10s %4d %8.2f\n", name, qty, price)
end
examples.output:
apple         3     0.50
watermelon    1     4.25
fig          12     0.33

sections.title: Formatting numbers with Printf

sections.body:
`open(path, "w") do io ... end` opens a file for writing, runs the block
with the stream `io`, and closes the file afterwards, even if the block
throws (the `do` + `finally` pattern from the errors unit). The modes:
`"r"` read (the default), `"w"` write (creates the file or **truncates** it),
`"a"` append to the end.

To read: `read(path, String)` returns the whole file, `readlines(path)` a
vector of lines without their newlines, and `eachline(path)` iterates over
the lines lazily, which is what you want for large files. `write(path, s)`
writes a whole string in one call.

`mktempdir()` creates a fresh temporary directory (removed when Julia exits),
which keeps examples from touching your own files. Its path differs on every
run and every system, so the examples print file *contents*, never paths.

examples.code:
dir = mktempdir()
path = joinpath(dir, "notes.txt")
open(path, "w") do io
    println(io, "first line")
    println(io, "second line")
end
open(path, "a") do io
    println(io, "appended")
end
print(read(path, String))
println(readlines(path))
for (i, line) in enumerate(eachline(path))
    println(i, ": ", line)
end
println(countlines(path), " lines, ", filesize(path), " bytes")
examples.output:
first line
second line
appended
["first line", "second line", "appended"]
1: first line
2: second line
3: appended
3 lines, 32 bytes

examples.caption: Mode `"w"` replaces what was there; `write(path, s)` returns the number of bytes written.
examples.code:
path = joinpath(mktempdir(), "data.txt")
println(write(path, "old content\n"))
open(path, "w") do io
    print(io, "new")
end
read(path, String)
examples.output:
12
"new"

sections.title: Reading and writing files

sections.body:
`print(x)` is `print(stdout, x)`. A program has a second output stream,
`stderr`, for diagnostics: `println(stderr, "warning: ...")`. Keeping
messages on `stderr` means the real output on `stdout` can be piped into a
file or another program without them. `@warn` and `@info` log to `stderr`.

`write(io, x)` writes raw bytes (for a string, its UTF-8 encoding) and
returns how many it wrote; `print` writes the text form. For strings the
result looks the same, but the count shows that `é` takes two bytes.
`redirect_stdout(f, io)` runs `f` with `stdout` pointed elsewhere (here
`devnull`, which discards everything), which is useful in tests.

examples.code:
n = write(stdout, "héllo\n")
println(n, " bytes for ", length("héllo\n"), " characters")
redirect_stdout(devnull) do
    println("this line goes nowhere")
end
println("back on stdout")
examples.output:
héllo
7 bytes for 6 characters
back on stdout

sections.title: stdout and stderr

sections.body:
For small, regular formats `split` and `parse` go a long way. `split(s, ',')`
returns `SubString`s (views into `s`, no copying); `strip` removes surrounding
whitespace; `parse(Int, s)` and `parse(Float64, s)` convert, throwing on bad
input (or use `tryparse`). `eachline(IOBuffer(text))` iterates over the lines
of a string just as `eachline(path)` does for a file.

Hand parsing is fine for configuration files and quick scripts; for real CSV
(quoted fields, embedded commas, missing values) use the CSV.jl package
(the data unit).

examples.code:
text = """
name,qty,price
apple,3,0.5
pear,10,0.25
fig,2,1.75
"""
lines = readlines(IOBuffer(text))
header = split(lines[1], ',')
total = 0.0
for line in lines[2:end]
    name, qty, price = split(line, ',')
    total += parse(Int, qty) * parse(Float64, price)
end
println(header, "  ", typeof(header))
println("total = ", total)
examples.output:
SubString{String}["name", "qty", "price"]  Vector{SubString{String}}
total = 7.5

(an `Int` matrix gives a `Vector{Int}`), and a matrix with no rows gives zeros.


The grader times your function on a 2000×2000 `Float64` matrix against a
reference that sums each column with Base's `sum` on a view (which uses SIMD
instructions). Mind the memory order and the allocations. A plain
column-by-column loop is correct but measures a few times slower than the
reference: it adds strictly in order, which the compiler may not reorder into
vector instructions unless you allow it (`@simd`). Float results are compared
with a relative tolerance, since summing in a different order changes the
last bits.

problems.title: Running maximum, in place

sections.body:
Julia compiles a function the first time you call it with a given combination
of argument types. So the **first** call of anything measures the compiler as
much as your code: `@time` reports that share as "compilation time". Always
call once to warm up, then measure, and repeat the measurement a few times and
keep the minimum (the least disturbed run). The package
[BenchmarkTools.jl](https://juliaci.github.io/BenchmarkTools.jl/stable/)
automates this with `@btime` and `@benchmark`; here we stay with Base.

Timings change from run to run and machine to machine, so the timing examples
on this page are recorded but not checked (the numbers you see are from one
run). Allocations are different: `@allocated` counts the bytes a call
allocates, and once the function is compiled that number is deterministic.
Measure it **inside a function**, after a warm-up call: at global scope the
measurement also counts the work of handling untyped global variables.

Later sections use a one-line helper for this:

```julia
measure(f::F, args...) where {F} = (f(args...); @allocated f(args...))
```

The `f::F ... where {F}` matters. Julia's heuristics sometimes decline to
specialise a method on a `Function` argument (here: one called with splatted
arguments), and the unspecialised call boxes its result. The type parameter
forces a specialised version, so the helper adds nothing to the count; written
as `measure(f, args...)` it reports 16 extra bytes for every call. The
[performance tips](https://docs.julialang.org/en/v1/manual/performance-tips/#Be-aware-of-when-Julia-avoids-specializing)
explain when this happens.

examples.output:
0.058258 seconds (28.08 k allocations: 1.935 MiB, 98.80% compilation time)

best of 20 runs: 196.1 μs

sections.title: Measuring without fooling yourself

sections.body:
A function is **type-stable** when the type of its result follows from the
types of its arguments alone, never from their values. Then the compiler knows
the type of every intermediate value and emits specialised machine code. When
it cannot know, it has to box values and look methods up at run time.

`Base.return_types(f, (ArgTypes...,))` asks the compiler what `f` returns. In
the REPL, `@code_warntype f(args...)` shows the inferred type of every local
variable and highlights the abstract ones (its output is long, so it is not
shown here; try it on your own functions).

The classic mistake is a literal of the wrong type: `0` is an `Int`, so a
function that returns `0` on one branch and a `Float64` on another returns a
`Union`. The fix is to build the constant from the argument: `zero(x)`,
`one(x)`, `zero(eltype(v))`. The same mistake hides in accumulators: `s = 0`
followed by `s += x` for floats makes `s` an `Int` before the loop and a
`Float64` after it, and an empty input returns the `Int`.

examples.caption: The return type depends on the *value* of `x`; `zero(x)` fixes it.
examples.code:
clamp_negative(x) = x < 0 ? 0 : x
clamp_negative_stable(x) = x < 0 ? zero(x) : x
println(Base.return_types(clamp_negative, (Float64,)))
println(Base.return_types(clamp_negative_stable, (Float64,)))
println(typeof(clamp_negative(-1.5)), " ", typeof(clamp_negative(1.5)))
examples.output:
Any[Union{Float64, Int64}]
Any[Float64]
Int64 Float64

examples.caption: An accumulator that starts as `0` and becomes a `Float64`; notice what the empty vector returns.
examples.code:
function total(v)
    s = 0                  # an Int ...
    for x in v
        s += x             # ... that becomes a Float64
    end
    return s
end
function total_stable(v)
    s = zero(eltype(v))    # 0.0 for a Vector{Float64}
    for x in v
        s += x
    end
    return s
end
println(Base.return_types(total, (Vector{Float64},)))
println(Base.return_types(total_stable, (Vector{Float64},)))
println(repr(total(Float64[])), "  ", repr(total_stable(Float64[])))
examples.output:
Any[Union{Float64, Int64}]
Any[Float64]
0  0.0

sections.title: Type stability

sections.body:
A non-`const` global variable can be rebound to a value of any type at any
moment, so a function that reads it cannot assume anything about its type:
the result is inferred as `Any`, and every operation on it is a dynamic
lookup. This is why "put your code in functions" is the first performance tip
in the [manual](https://docs.julialang.org/en/v1/manual/performance-tips/).
Three fixes, from most to least common:

* pass the value as an **argument** (the function is then compiled for its type);
* declare it `const` if it really never changes;
* give the global a **type** (Julia 1.8 and later): `rate::Float64 = 1.5`. Its
  value can still change, but only to another `Float64`.

Python and MATLAB users write scripts full of top-level loops over globals;
in Julia the same loop inside a function is often tens of times faster.

examples.caption: Reading an untyped global makes the result `Any`; `const` or an argument makes it concrete.
examples.code:
rate = 1.5
scale(v) = sum(x * rate for x in v)
const RATE = 1.5
scale_const(v) = sum(x * RATE for x in v)
scale_arg(v, r) = sum(x * r for x in v)
println(Base.return_types(scale, (Vector{Float64},)))
println(Base.return_types(scale_const, (Vector{Float64},)))
println(Base.return_types(scale_arg, (Vector{Float64}, Float64)))
examples.output:
Any[Any]
Any[Float64]
Any[Float64]

examples.caption: A typed global: the type is fixed, the value is not. Assigning `2` converts it; a string cannot be converted.
examples.code:
rate::Float64 = 1.5
scale(v) = sum(x * rate for x in v)
println(Base.return_types(scale, (Vector{Float64},)))
rate = 2
println(rate)
rate = "fast"
examples.output:
Any[Float64]
2.0
ERROR: MethodError: Cannot `convert` an object of type String to an object of type Float64

Closest candidates are:
  convert(::Type{T}, !Matched::T) where T<:Number
   @ Base number.jl:6
  convert(::Type{T}, !Matched::CartesianIndex{1}) where T<:Number
   @ Base multidimensional.jl:135
  convert(::Type{T}, !Matched::AbstractChar) where T<:Number
   @ Base char.jl:185
  ...

  @ top-level scope at line 6

examples.caption: The same loop over a global and over an argument: count the bytes allocated.
examples.code:
data = rand(1000)
function sum_global()
    s = 0.0
    for x in data          # `data` could be anything: every step is dynamic
        s += x
    end
    return s
end
function sum_arg(v)
    s = 0.0
    for x in v
        s += x
    end
    return s
end
measure(f::F, args...) where {F} = (f(args...); @allocated f(args...))
println("global:   ", measure(sum_global), " bytes")
println("argument: ", measure(sum_arg, data), " bytes")
examples.output:
global:   71840 bytes
argument: 0 bytes

sections.title: Global variables

sections.body:
A `Vector{Float64}` stores the numbers themselves, side by side in memory. A
`Vector{Any}` or a `Vector{Real}` stores *pointers* to boxed values, because
its elements may have different types and sizes; every access then follows a
pointer and dispatches at run time. `isconcretetype` tells you whether a type
can be the type of an actual value: `Float64` can, `Real` cannot.

The same applies to struct fields. A field declared `x::Real` can hold any
real number, so code that reads it cannot be specialised. Make the struct
**parametric** instead: `struct Point{T<:Real}; x::T; end` creates a separate
concrete type `Point{Float64}`, `Point{Int64}`, … for each field type, with
the same flexibility and none of the cost.

examples.caption: Same numbers, three containers. `sum` over the abstract ones allocates a box for each intermediate result.
examples.code:
measure(f::F, args...) where {F} = (f(args...); @allocated f(args...))
a = rand(1000)
b = Vector{Any}(a)
c = Vector{Real}(a)
println(isconcretetype(eltype(a)), " ", isconcretetype(eltype(b)), " ", isconcretetype(eltype(c)))
println("Vector{Float64}: ", measure(sum, a), " bytes")
println("Vector{Any} allocates:  ", measure(sum, b) > 0)
println("Vector{Real} allocates: ", measure(sum, c) > 0)
examples.output:
true false false
Vector{Float64}: 0 bytes
Vector{Any} allocates:  true
Vector{Real} allocates: true

examples.caption: An abstract field makes `norm2` return `Any`; a type parameter keeps it concrete.
examples.code:
struct PointAbstract
    x::Real
    y::Real
end
struct Point{T<:Real}
    x::T
    y::T
end
norm2(p) = p.x^2 + p.y^2
println(Base.return_types(norm2, (PointAbstract,)))
println(Base.return_types(norm2, (Point{Float64},)))
println(typeof(Point(3.0, 4.0)), " ", typeof(Point(3, 4)))
norm2(Point(3.0, 4.0))
examples.output:
Any[Any]
Any[Float64]
Point{Float64} Point{Int64}
25.0

sections.title: Concrete element types and fields

sections.body:
Allocating memory is not free, and the garbage collector must later reclaim
it. Three sources dominate in numerical code.

**Slices copy.** Unlike NumPy, `x[2:end-1]` creates a new array (MATLAB and R
copy too). `@view x[2:end-1]` creates a lightweight window into `x` instead,
and `@views` in front of a function or block turns every slice in it into a
view. Mutating a view mutates the parent.

**Every vectorised operation makes an array**, unless you fuse it. `2x + x.^2`
makes three arrays (one per operation); the dotted `2 .* x .+ x .^ 2` fuses
into a single loop with a single result array; and `out .= 2 .* x .+ x .^ 2`
(or `@. out = 2x + x^2`) writes into an existing array and allocates nothing.

**Preallocate and update in place.** Functions whose names end in `!` modify
an argument instead of returning a new value: `mul!(C, A, B)` from
`LinearAlgebra` writes `A * B` into `C`, `sort!`, `push!`, `copyto!`, `fill!`.
In a loop that runs many times, allocate the output once outside it.

In the last example a 1000-element `Vector{Float64}` costs 8128 bytes (8000
for the data plus the array header): the unfused version allocates three of
them, the fused one a single array (plus 16 bytes of bookkeeping), the
in-place one nothing; `A * B` allocates the 50×50 result, `mul!` nothing.

examples.caption: A slice is a copy; a view is a window into the original array.
examples.code:
x = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
s = x[2:4]          # a new array
v = @view x[2:4]    # a view of x
s[1] = 100          # changes only the copy
v[2] = 300          # changes x[3]
x
examples.output:
5-element Vector{Int64}:
   1
   2
 300
   4
   5

examples.caption: The copy allocates the whole slice; the views allocate nothing.
examples.code:
measure(f::F, args...) where {F} = (f(args...); @allocated f(args...))
inner_sum_copy(x) = sum(x[2:end-1])
inner_sum_view(x) = sum(@view x[2:end-1])
@views inner_sum_views(x) = sum(x[2:end-1])
x = rand(1000)
println(measure(inner_sum_copy, x), " ", measure(inner_sum_view, x), " ", measure(inner_sum_views, x))

examples.caption: Unfused, fused and in-place broadcasting, then `*` against `mul!`.
examples.code:
using LinearAlgebra
measure(f::F, args...) where {F} = (f(args...); @allocated f(args...))
unfused(x) = 2x + x .^ 2                  # three arrays
fused(x) = 2 .* x .+ x .^ 2               # one loop, one array
inplace!(out, x) = (out .= 2 .* x .+ x .^ 2; out)   # no new array
x = rand(1000); out = similar(x)
println(measure(unfused, x), " ", measure(fused, x), " ", measure(inplace!, out, x))
A = rand(50, 50); B = rand(50, 50); C = similar(A)
println(measure(*, A, B), " ", measure(mul!, C, A, B))
C ≈ A * B

sections.title: Allocations: slices, views, fusion and in-place updates

sections.body:
Loops are fast in Julia (unlike in Python or R there is no need to vectorise
for speed), but the processor still rewards some habits.

**Arrays are column-major**, like Fortran and MATLAB and unlike C and NumPy's
default: `A[1,1]`, `A[2,1]`, `A[3,1]`, … are adjacent in memory. Make the
*first* index vary fastest, i.e. put the row loop inside the column loop.
Walking along rows jumps through memory and wastes most of every cache line
fetched; the gap grows with the matrix.

**Do not repeat work in the inner loop.** A value that does not change inside
the loop (a norm, a length, a lookup) belongs before it. Recomputing an O(n)
quantity n times turns an O(n) function into an O(n²) one.

**`@inbounds` and `@simd`.** Every `x[i]` checks that `i` is a valid index.
`@inbounds` removes the check, and `@simd` lets the compiler reorder a
reduction so it can use vector instructions (so a floating-point sum may
differ in the last bits). Write and test the bounds-checked version first:
with checks on, a wrong index is a `BoundsError`; under `@inbounds` it is
**undefined behaviour**, i.e. garbage results or a crash, not an error. Prefer
`eachindex(x)` over `1:length(x)`: it is always valid, so the compiler can
often drop the checks by itself.

examples.caption: `vec` shows the memory order: down the first column, then the second.
examples.output:
6-element Vector{Int64}:
 1
 4
 2
 5
 3
 6

examples.caption: The same sum, two loop orders, on a 2000×2000 matrix. Recorded, not checked: timings vary.
examples.code:
function sum_by_columns(A)
    s = zero(eltype(A))
    for j in axes(A, 2), i in axes(A, 1)    # i (rows) varies fastest
        s += A[i, j]
    end
    return s
end
function sum_by_rows(A)
    s = zero(eltype(A))
    for i in axes(A, 1), j in axes(A, 2)    # j varies fastest: strided access
        s += A[i, j]
    end
    return s
end
A = rand(2000, 2000)
sum_by_columns(A); sum_by_rows(A)
t_col = minimum(@elapsed(sum_by_columns(A)) for _ in 1:5)
t_row = minimum(@elapsed(sum_by_rows(A)) for _ in 1:5)
println("columns: ", round(t_col * 1e3; digits = 1), " ms, rows: ", round(t_row * 1e3; digits = 1), " ms")
examples.output: columns: 4.7 ms, rows: 16.4 ms

examples.caption: A norm recomputed inside the loop makes the function quadratic. Same result, very different time (not checked).
examples.code:
function normalize_slow(v)
    out = similar(v)
    for i in eachindex(v)
        out[i] = v[i] / sqrt(sum(abs2, v))   # O(n) work, n times
    end
    return out
end
function normalize_fast(v)
    nrm = sqrt(sum(abs2, v))                # once, before the loop
    out = similar(v)
    for i in eachindex(v)
        out[i] = v[i] / nrm
    end
    return out
end
v = rand(20_000)
println(normalize_slow(v) == normalize_fast(v))
t_slow = @elapsed normalize_slow(v)
t_fast = @elapsed normalize_fast(v)
println("slow: ", round(t_slow * 1e3; digits = 2), " ms, fast: ", round(t_fast * 1e3; digits = 3), " ms")
examples.output:
true
slow: 44.17 ms, fast: 0.068 ms

examples.caption: First the bounds-checked version: an off-by-one index is caught as a `BoundsError`.
examples.code:
function mysum(x)
    s = zero(eltype(x))
    for i in 1:length(x) + 1      # bug: one past the end
        s += x[i]
    end
    return s
end
mysum([1.0, 2.0, 3.0])
examples.output:
ERROR: BoundsError: attempt to access 3-element Vector{Float64} at index [4]
  @ mysum at line 4
  @ top-level scope at line 8

examples.caption: Once the indices are right (`eachindex`), `@inbounds @simd` is safe. The reordered sum agrees with `sum` up to rounding; the speed-up is not checked.
examples.code:
function mysum_simd(x)
    s = zero(eltype(x))
    @inbounds @simd for i in eachindex(x)
        s += x[i]
    end
    return s
end
function mysum_plain(x)
    s = zero(eltype(x))
    for i in eachindex(x)
        s += x[i]
    end
    return s
end
x = rand(10^6)
println(mysum_simd(x) ≈ sum(x), " ", mysum_plain(x) ≈ sum(x))
mysum_simd(x); mysum_plain(x)
t_simd = minimum(@elapsed(mysum_simd(x)) for _ in 1:10)
t_plain = minimum(@elapsed(mysum_plain(x)) for _ in 1:10)
println("@simd: ", round(t_simd * 1e6; digits = 1), " μs, plain: ", round(t_plain * 1e6; digits = 1), " μs")
examples.output:
true true
@simd: 164.9 μs, plain: 1137.0 μs

sections.title: Loops: memory order, hoisting, @inbounds and @simd

sections.body:
Sometimes a type really is unknown until run time: a value read from a file,
a `Dict{String,Any}` of columns, a user's choice. You cannot make that one
lookup type-stable, but you can stop the uncertainty from spreading. Do the
lookup in a small outer function and hand the value to a **kernel function**
that does the real work. Calling the kernel costs one dynamic dispatch; inside
it, Julia compiles a specialised version for the actual type, so the loop is
fast. This pattern is called a *function barrier*.

In the example, `sum_of_column` loops over a value of type `Any`; `kernel` is
inferred concretely for a `Vector{Float64}`, and `sum_with_barrier` only adds
one dispatch in front of it. (Timings recorded, not checked.)

examples.code:
function sum_of_column(table::Dict{String,Any}, name)
    col = table[name]                 # type known only at run time
    s = zero(eltype(col))
    for x in col                      # every step is a dynamic call
        s += x
    end
    return s
end
function kernel(col)
    s = zero(eltype(col))
    for x in col
        s += x
    end
    return s
end
sum_with_barrier(table, name) = kernel(table[name])

table = Dict{String,Any}("price" => rand(10^6), "count" => rand(1:9, 10^6))
println(Base.return_types(sum_of_column, (Dict{String,Any}, String)))
println(Base.return_types(kernel, (Vector{Float64},)))
println(sum_of_column(table, "price") == sum_with_barrier(table, "price"))
sum_of_column(table, "price"); sum_with_barrier(table, "price")
t1 = minimum(@elapsed(sum_of_column(table, "price")) for _ in 1:5)
t2 = minimum(@elapsed(sum_with_barrier(table, "price")) for _ in 1:5)
println("no barrier: ", round(t1 * 1e3; digits = 2), " ms, barrier: ", round(t2 * 1e3; digits = 2), " ms")
examples.output:
Any[Any]
Any[Float64]
true
no barrier: 61.66 ms, barrier: 0.86 ms

sections.title: Function barriers

units.summary: How to measure Julia code without fooling yourself, and the handful of habits that make it fast: type-stable functions, no untyped globals, concrete containers and fields, few allocations, memory-order loops and function barriers.
units.title: Performance: measuring, type stability and allocations

hints: Start the sum at a zero of the right type. Which function gives the type of `x[i] * y[i]` from the two element types?
`zero(promote_type(eltype(x), eltype(y)))`; and `eachindex(x, y)` gives the common indices, throwing a `DimensionMismatch` when they differ.
problems.prompt:
Write `generic_dot(x, y)` returning `x[1]*y[1] + x[2]*y[2] + …` for two
vectors of real numbers of **any** element types (integers, floats,
rationals, ranges too), possibly different from each other.

* The result has the promoted type: `Int` and `Float64` give a `Float64`,
  `Rational{Int}` and `Int` give a `Rational{Int}`.
* Two empty vectors give a zero of that type: `generic_dot(Int[], Float64[])`
  is `0.0`.
* Vectors of different lengths throw a `DimensionMismatch`.

```julia
generic_dot([1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6])      # 32
generic_dot([1//2, 1//3], [2, 3])      # 2//1
```

Do not use `LinearAlgebra.dot`: the point is to write the generic loop.
problems.title: A generic dot product

hints: Once `promote_rule` and `convert` exist, `s * t + c` with a dual `s * t` and a plain `c` promotes `c` to a dual for you.
`convert(::Type{Dual{T}}, x::Real) where {T<:Real} = Dual{T}(x, zero(T))`, and start Horner's rule from a dual zero of the promoted type `T`.
problems.prompt:
A **dual number** `a + b·ε` with `ε² = 0` carries a value and a derivative:
`(a, a′) + (b, b′) = (a + b, a′ + b′)` and `(a, a′) · (b, b′) = (a·b, a′·b + a·b′)`
(the product rule). Evaluate a polynomial at the dual number `(x, 1)` and you
get `(p(x), p′(x))` exactly; this is forward-mode automatic differentiation.

1. Define `struct Dual{T<:Real} <: Number` with fields `val::T` and `der::T`,
   and `Base.:+` and `Base.:*` for two duals.
2. Add `Base.convert` and `Base.promote_rule` so that a dual plus a plain
   number works (a plain number `c` is the dual `(c, 0)`).
3. Write `value_and_derivative(coeffs, x)` that evaluates
   `coeffs[1] + coeffs[2]*x + coeffs[3]*x^2 + …` (at least one coefficient) at
   a dual number with Horner's rule (`s = s*t + c`, from the last coefficient
   to the first) and returns the tuple `(p(x), p′(x))` of plain numbers.

Both results have the promoted type of the coefficients and `x`:

```julia
value_and_derivative([1, 2, 3], 2)        # (17, 14)
value_and_derivative([0, 0, 1], 1//2)     # (1//4, 1//1)
value_and_derivative([1.0, 2.0], 3)       # (7.0, 2.0)
```

Results are compared exactly (tuples have no `isapprox`); Horner's rule on
duals gives exactly the reference's floating-point values.
problems.starter:
struct Dual{T<:Real} <: Number
    val::T
    der::T
end

function value_and_derivative(coeffs, x)
    # your code here
end
problems.title: Derivatives with dual numbers

sections.body:
A method signature can name the types it receives: in
`f(v::AbstractVector{T}) where {T}` the *type parameter* `T` is bound to the
element type of the argument, and you can use it in the body like any value.
`where {T<:Real}` restricts it. Writing the same parameter twice,
`f(x::T, y::T) where {T}`, means "both arguments have the same type".

One rule surprises everyone: parametric types are **invariant**. A
`Vector{Int}` is *not* a `Vector{Real}`, even though `Int <: Real`, because a
`Vector{Real}` is a specific container that can hold any mix of reals (see the
performance unit for why it is slow). To accept "a vector of any real type",
write `AbstractVector{<:Real}`, short for `AbstractVector{T} where {T<:Real}`.

examples.code:
elementtype(v::AbstractVector{T}) where {T} = T
sametype(x::T, y::T) where {T} = true
sametype(x, y) = false
println(elementtype([1, 2]), " ", elementtype(["a"]), " ", elementtype(1.0:2.0))
println(sametype(1, 2), " ", sametype(1, 2.0))
examples.output:
Int64 String Float64
true false

examples.caption: Invariance: `Vector{Real}` accepts only a `Vector{Real}`; `AbstractVector{<:Real}` accepts every real vector.
examples.code:
println(Vector{Int} <: Vector{Real}, " ", Vector{Int} <: Vector{<:Real}, " ", Vector{Int} <: AbstractVector{<:Real})
total_any(v::AbstractVector{<:Real}) = sum(v)
total_real(v::Vector{Real}) = sum(v)
println(total_any([1, 2, 3]), " ", total_any(0.5:0.5:2))
total_real([1, 2, 3])
examples.output:
false true true
6 5.0
ERROR: MethodError: no method matching total_real(::Vector{Int64})

Closest candidates are:
  total_real(!Matched::Vector{Real})
   @ Main main.jl:3

  @ top-level scope at line 5

sections.title: Parametric methods

sections.body:
Coming from C or Java, it is tempting to annotate every argument. In Julia it
does not make the code faster: the compiler specialises a method for the
concrete types it is *called* with, annotated or not. `double(x) = 2x`
called with a `Float64` compiles to the same single multiplication as
`double(x::Float64) = 2x`, and it keeps working for integers, rationals,
`BigFloat`s and types that do not exist yet.

Annotate to **choose between methods** (dispatch), or to document and
reject what makes no sense. Over-narrow annotations such as `::Float64` or
`::Vector{Float64}` are a common reason a package refuses an `Int`, a range,
a view or a `Float32` that would have worked.

examples.caption: The untyped method, compiled for a `Float64`: one multiplication, inferred `Float64`.
examples.code:
double(x) = 2x
code_typed(double, (Float64,))
examples.output:
1-element Vector{Any}:
 CodeInfo(
1 ─ %1 = Base.mul_float(2.0, x)::Float64
└──      return %1
) => Float64

examples.code:
double(x) = 2x
double_float(x::Float64) = 2x
println(double(3), " ", double(1//3), " ", double(0.25f0), " ", double(big"1.5"))
double_float(3)
examples.output:
6 2//3 0.5 3.0
ERROR: MethodError: no method matching double_float(::Int64)

Closest candidates are:
  double_float(!Matched::Float64)
   @ Main main.jl:2

  @ top-level scope at line 4

sections.title: Annotations are for dispatch, not speed

examples.code:
function mysum(v)
    s = zero(eltype(v))
    for x in v
        s += x
    end
    return s
end
println(mysum([1, 2, 3]), " | ", mysum([0.5, 0.25]), " | ", mysum([1//2, 1//3]), " | ", mysum([1 + 2im, 3im]))
println(repr(mysum(Int[])), " | ", repr(mysum(Float32[])), " | ", repr(mysum(Rational{Int}[])))

examples.caption: `similar` makes the output; `promote_type` names the type of a mixed result.
examples.code:
function prefix_sums(v)
    out = similar(v, eltype(v), length(v))
    s = zero(eltype(v))
    for (i, x) in enumerate(v)
        s += x
        out[i] = s
    end
    return out
end
println(prefix_sums([1, 2, 3]), " ", prefix_sums(0.5:0.5:1.5), " ", prefix_sums([1//2, 1//4]))
println(promote_type(Int, Float64), " ", promote_type(Int, Rational{Int}), " ", promote_type(Float32, Int), " ", promote_type(Int8, Int16))
examples.output:
[1, 3, 6] [0.5, 1.5, 3.0] Rational{Int64}[1//2, 3//4]
Float64 Rational{Int64} Float32 Int16

sections.title: Writing generic code: zero, one, eltype, similar, promote_type

sections.body:
`struct Interval{T<:Real}` defines a family of concrete types,
`Interval{Int64}`, `Interval{Float64}`, …, with concretely typed fields.
Constructors come in two kinds:

* an **inner constructor** (inside the `struct`, calling `new`) is the only
  way to create the object, so it is the place to enforce an invariant such as
  `lo ≤ hi`;
* **outer constructors** are ordinary methods that add conveniences: here
  `Interval(1, 3)` infers `T` from the arguments, and `Interval(1, 2.5)`
  promotes mixed arguments to a common type first.

Once you write an inner constructor, Julia no longer defines the default
ones, which is why the outer `Interval(lo::T, hi::T)` is needed.

examples.code:
struct Interval{T<:Real}
    lo::T
    hi::T
    function Interval{T}(lo, hi) where {T<:Real}
        lo <= hi || throw(ArgumentError("need lo ≤ hi, got $lo > $hi"))
        return new{T}(lo, hi)
    end
end
Interval(lo::T, hi::T) where {T<:Real} = Interval{T}(lo, hi)
Interval(lo::Real, hi::Real) = Interval(promote(lo, hi)...)
width(i::Interval) = i.hi - i.lo

println(Interval(1, 3), " ", Interval(1, 2.5))
println(width(Interval(1//2, 3//4)))
Interval(3, 1)
examples.output:
Interval{Int64}(1, 3) Interval{Float64}(1.0, 2.5)
1//4
ERROR: ArgumentError: need lo ≤ hi, got 3 > 1
  @ Interval at line 5
  @ Interval at line 9
  @ top-level scope at line 15

sections.title: Parametric structs and their constructors

sections.body:
Arithmetic between different types in Julia goes through **promotion**:
`1 + 2.5` has no special method; the fallback `+(x::Number, y::Number)` calls
`promote(x, y)` to convert both to a common type, then adds those. To make
your own type join in, write

* the operations between two values of your type (`Base.:+`, `Base.:*`, …);
* `Base.promote_rule(::Type{Mine}, ::Type{Other})`: the common type;
* `Base.convert(::Type{Mine}, x::Other)`: how to convert.

You extend Base's functions (`Base.:+`), you do not shadow them; that is how
`sum`, `prod`, `^` and every generic algorithm start working on the new type.
Below, integers modulo `N` with `N` a type parameter: `Mod{7}` and `Mod{5}`
are different types, and mixing them is an error (no promotion rule
between them) rather than a silent bug.

examples.caption: Operations between two `Mod{N}` values work; `a + 1` fails because there is no promotion rule yet: `promote` cannot find a common type.
examples.code:
struct Mod{N} <: Number
    val::Int
    Mod{N}(x::Integer) where {N} = new(mod(x, N))
end
Base.:+(a::Mod{N}, b::Mod{N}) where {N} = Mod{N}(a.val + b.val)
Base.:*(a::Mod{N}, b::Mod{N}) where {N} = Mod{N}(a.val * b.val)
Base.show(io::IO, a::Mod{N}) where {N} = print(io, a.val, " (mod ", N, ")")

a = Mod{7}(5)
println(a + Mod{7}(4), ", ", a * a)
a + 1
examples.output:
2 (mod 7), 4 (mod 7)
ERROR: promotion of types Mod{7} and Int64 failed to change any arguments
  @ top-level scope at line 11

examples.caption: With `promote_rule` and `convert`, integers mix in, and generic functions (`sum`, `^`) work unchanged.
examples.code:
struct Mod{N} <: Number
    val::Int
    Mod{N}(x::Integer) where {N} = new(mod(x, N))
end
Base.:+(a::Mod{N}, b::Mod{N}) where {N} = Mod{N}(a.val + b.val)
Base.:*(a::Mod{N}, b::Mod{N}) where {N} = Mod{N}(a.val * b.val)
Base.show(io::IO, a::Mod{N}) where {N} = print(io, a.val, " (mod ", N, ")")
Base.promote_rule(::Type{Mod{N}}, ::Type{<:Integer}) where {N} = Mod{N}
Base.convert(::Type{Mod{N}}, x::Integer) where {N} = Mod{N}(x)

a = Mod{7}(5)
println(a + 1, ", ", 3 * a, ", ", a^3)
println(sum([Mod{7}(3), Mod{7}(6), Mod{7}(1)]))
a + Mod{5}(1)
examples.output:
6 (mod 7), 1 (mod 7), 6 (mod 7)
3 (mod 7)
ERROR: promotion of types Mod{7} and Mod{5} failed to change any arguments
  @ top-level scope at line 14

sections.title: A number-like type and promotion

sections.body:
Julia supports two styles of generic code, and good code uses both.

**Duck typing**: leave arguments unannotated and use only the operations you
need. `describe(x)` below calls `length` and `first`, so it works for arrays,
strings, tuples, dicts, even a number (numbers are iterable collections of one
element), with no declaration anywhere.

**Dispatch on abstract types** picks a method by what a type *is*:
`AbstractVector`, `AbstractString`, `Number`. But a type has only one
supertype, and many properties cut across the hierarchy ("is it sorted?",
"is its length known?"). For those Julia uses **Holy traits** (after Tim
Holy): a function from a *type* to a small singleton object, and methods that
dispatch on that object. Base does this with `Base.IteratorSize`, which
`collect` uses to decide whether it can preallocate. The trait is computed from
the type, so the compiler resolves the choice at compile time: there is no
run-time check left.

examples.code:
describe(x) = "$(length(x)) item(s), first: $(repr(first(x)))"
println(describe([3, 1, 2]))
println(describe("hello"))
println(describe((a = 1, b = 2)))
println(describe(42))
examples.output:
3 item(s), first: 3
5 item(s), first: 'h'
2 item(s), first: 1
1 item(s), first: 42

examples.caption: Base's trait: what `collect` knows about an iterator's length.
examples.code:
println(Base.IteratorSize([1, 2, 3]))
println(Base.IteratorSize(x^2 for x in 1:3))
println(Base.IteratorSize(Iterators.filter(iseven, 1:10)))
println(Base.IteratorSize(Iterators.countfrom(1)))
examples.output:
Base.HasShape{1}()
Base.HasShape{1}()
Base.SizeUnknown()
Base.IsInfinite()

examples.caption: A custom trait: ranges declare themselves sorted, so `mymedian` skips the sort for them.
examples.code:
abstract type Sortedness end
struct KnownSorted <: Sortedness end
struct MaybeUnsorted <: Sortedness end
sortedness(::Type) = MaybeUnsorted()
sortedness(::Type{<:AbstractRange}) = KnownSorted()

mymedian(x) = mymedian(sortedness(typeof(x)), x)
function mymedian(::KnownSorted, x)
    n = length(x)
    return (x[(n + 1) ÷ 2] + x[n ÷ 2 + 1]) / 2
end
mymedian(::MaybeUnsorted, x) = mymedian(KnownSorted(), sort(x))

println(sortedness(typeof(1:10)), " ", sortedness(typeof([3, 1, 2])))
println(mymedian(1:10), " ", mymedian([5, 1, 4]), " ", mymedian([7, 1, 3, 2]))
examples.output:
KnownSorted() MaybeUnsorted()
5.5 4.0 2.5

sections.title: Duck typing, abstract types and Holy traits

sections.body:
`Val(3)` is an instance of the type `Val{3}`: it moves a value into the type
domain, so methods can dispatch on it and the compiler can treat it as a
constant. `ntuple(f, Val(4))` builds a tuple whose length is known at compile
time; `Val(:fast)` can select an algorithm by name.

Use it only when the value is a **literal at the call site**. `Val(n)` with an
`n` computed at run time creates a type the compiler could not predict, so the
call becomes a dynamic dispatch and is slower than an ordinary argument. For
most choices a plain argument or a keyword is the right tool.

examples.code:
println(ntuple(i -> i^2, Val(4)), " ", typeof(Val(4)))
power(x, ::Val{N}) where {N} = x^N
println(power(2.0, Val(3)))
algorithm(::Val{:fast}, x) = "fast path for $x"
algorithm(::Val{:safe}, x) = "safe path for $x"
println(algorithm(Val(:fast), 1))
algorithm(Val(:other), 1)
examples.output:
(1, 4, 9, 16) Val{4}
8.0
fast path for 1
ERROR: MethodError: no method matching algorithm(::Val{:other}, ::Int64)

Closest candidates are:
  algorithm(!Matched::Val{:safe}, ::Any)
   @ Main main.jl:5
  algorithm(!Matched::Val{:fast}, ::Any)
   @ Main main.jl:4

  @ top-level scope at line 7

hints: Keep a `Dict{Symbol,Int}` of counts and visit every sub-expression in `ex.args`, recursively.
Write a helper with two methods: one for `ex::Expr` (count `ex.args[1]` when `ex.head == :call` and it is a `Symbol`, then recurse into every argument), one for anything else that does nothing.
problems.prompt:
Write `call_counts(ex)` that walks the expression `ex` and counts, for every
function called by name, how many times it is called. A call is an `Expr`
with head `:call`; its first argument is the function (count it only when it
is a `Symbol`); calls nested inside arguments count too. Return the counts as
a vector of `name => count` pairs sorted by name (`sort!(collect(dict))`), so
the order does not depend on a `Dict`'s internal layout.

```julia
call_counts(:(sin(x) + sin(y) * 2))   # [:* => 1, :+ => 1, :sin => 2]
call_counts(:x)                       # Pair{Symbol, Int64}[]
```

`ex.args` is a `Vector{Any}`: anything can be in it. Recursion with one method
for `Expr` and one for everything else lets dispatch sort that out.
problems.title: Count the function calls in an expression

hints: Rebuild the tree: a new `Expr` with the same `head` and every argument substituted, recursively.
Write methods for `Symbol` (replace it when it is `var`), for `Expr` (`Expr(e.head, (... for a in e.args)...)`), and for anything else (return it unchanged).
problems.prompt:
Write `substitute(ex, var, val)` that returns a **new** expression in which
every occurrence of the symbol `var` in the `Expr` `ex` (at any depth) is
replaced by `val`. The original `ex` must not change: the grader checks it
after the call.

```julia
substitute(:(x^2 + 2x + 1), :x, 3)        # :(3 ^ 2 + 2 * 3 + 1)
eval(substitute(:(x^2 + 2x + 1), :x, 3))  # 16
substitute(:(exp(x) + y), :x, :(a + b))   # :(exp(a + b) + y)
```

Expressions are compared with `isequal`, which compares the trees. Turning
the expression into a string and back is not a correct shortcut (try `exp`).
As in the previous problem, a helper with one method per kind of node
(`Symbol`, `Expr`, anything else) keeps `Any`-typed variables out of your
entry function; the grader checks its types.
problems.title: Substitute a value for a symbol

sections.body:
Before Julia runs your code it parses it into a data structure you can
inspect and build yourself. A **`Symbol`** is an interned name: `:x` is the
symbol `x` (and `Symbol("x")` makes the same one). An **`Expr`** has a
`head` saying what kind of expression it is (`:call`, `:(=)`, `:block`,
`:if`, …) and a vector `args` of sub-expressions, which can be symbols,
literals or further `Expr`s.

`Meta.parse` turns a string into an expression, and `dump` prints the tree.
Notice that an operator call `a + 1` is just a `:call` whose first argument is
the function's name `:+`.

examples.code:
ex = Meta.parse("a + b * 2")
println(typeof(ex), " ", ex.head, " ", ex.args)
println(typeof(:a), " ", :a === Symbol("a"))
dump(:(a + 1))
examples.output:
Expr call Any[:+, :a, :(b * 2)]
Symbol true
Expr
  head: Symbol call
  args: Array{Any}((3,))
    1: Symbol +
    2: Symbol a
    3: Int64 1

sections.title: Symbols and expressions

sections.body:
`:( ... )` *quotes* code: it returns the expression instead of evaluating it.
For several lines, `quote ... end` does the same and produces a `:block`
expression; it also records source positions as `LineNumberNode`s (the
`#= main.jl:3 =#` comments in the display), which
`Base.remove_linenums!` strips.

Inside a quote, `$` **interpolates**: `:($x + 1)` puts the *value* of `x`
into the expression, while `:(x + 1)` keeps the symbol. `$(args...)` splices
a list of arguments. You can also build expressions directly with
`Expr(head, args...)`, which is what quoting does for you.

examples.code:
ex1 = :(x + 1)
ex2 = quote
    y = x + 1
    y * 2
end
println(typeof(ex1), " ", ex1.head, " ", ex2.head)
ex2
examples.output:
Expr call block
quote
    #= main.jl:3 =#
    y = x + 1
    #= main.jl:4 =#
    y * 2
end

examples.code:
x = 10
println(:(x + 1), "   ", :($x + 1))
args = [:a, :b, :c]
println(:(f($(args...))))
println(Expr(:call, :+, 1, 2) == :(1 + 2))
examples.output:
x + 1   10 + 1
f(a, b, c)
true

sections.title: Quoting and interpolation

sections.body:
`eval(ex)` evaluates an expression **in the global scope of the current
module**. At the top level that is useful: it can define variables or
functions whose names are computed (`eval(:($name = 42)))`).

Inside a function `eval` is almost always a mistake. It cannot see the
function's local variables (they do not exist in global scope), it compiles
the expression anew on every call, and its result has a type the compiler
cannot know. If you find yourself writing `eval` inside a function, you
usually want a closure, a `Dict` from names to functions, or dispatch.

examples.code:
ex = :(2 + 3 * 4)
println(eval(ex))
name = :answer
eval(:($name = 42))
answer

examples.caption: `eval` runs in global scope, so the local `y` is invisible to it.
examples.output:
ERROR: UndefVarError: `y` not defined
  @ add_one_with_eval at line 2
  @ top-level scope at line 4

sections.title: eval, and why not inside functions

sections.body:
A **macro** is a function that runs when the code is *parsed*: it receives
its arguments as expressions (unevaluated) and returns a new expression that
replaces the macro call. `@macroexpand` shows that replacement, which is the
first thing to look at when a macro misbehaves.

Macros are **hygienic**: variables that the macro's own code assigns are
renamed (to fresh names from `gensym`) so they cannot clash with the
caller's, and other names are looked up in the module where the macro was
defined. Code that comes from the *caller* must be wrapped in `esc(...)` so
that it keeps its meaning in the caller's scope. Forgetting `esc` is the
classic macro bug. In the second example the unescaped `x` in `x *= 3` is
resolved in the macro's module, as the global `Main.x`, and an expansion may
not assign to a module-qualified name: the error points at the macro call.

examples.code:
macro twice(ex)
    return quote
        $(esc(ex))
        $(esc(ex))
    end
end
x = 1
@twice x *= 3
println(x)
Base.remove_linenums!(@macroexpand @twice x *= 3)
examples.output:
9
quote
    x *= 3
    x *= 3
end

examples.caption: Without `esc`, the caller's `x` is read as a name in the macro's module.
examples.code:
macro twice_unescaped(ex)
    return quote
        $ex
        $ex
    end
end
x = 1
@twice_unescaped x *= 3
examples.output:
ERROR: syntax: invalid assignment location "Main.x" around main.jl:3
  @ top-level scope at line 8

examples.caption: Hygiene protects the caller: the macro's own `n` is a different variable.
examples.code:
macro repeat3(ex)
    return quote
        n = 0
        for _ in 1:3
            $(esc(ex))
            n += 1
        end
        n
    end
end
n = 100
r = @repeat3 print("hi ")
println()
println(r, " ", n)
examples.output:
hi hi hi 
3 100

sections.title: Macros, esc and hygiene

sections.body:
Macros earn their place when they need the *code itself*, not only its
value: to skip evaluating it, to evaluate it differently, or to print it.
`@unless cond body` evaluates `body` only when `cond` is false, which no
function can do (a function's arguments are evaluated before it is called).
`@logcall f(args...)` prints the call as written in the source together with
the argument values, then makes the call. Note how it checks its input and
raises a clear error at expansion time for anything that is not a call.

examples.output:
low balance: 5
:(if !(balance > 10)
      println("low")
  end)

examples.code:
macro logcall(ex)
    (ex isa Expr && ex.head == :call) || error("@logcall expects a function call, got $(repr(ex))")
    f = ex.args[1]
    args = ex.args[2:end]
    return quote
        local vals = ($(map(esc, args)...),)
        println("call ", $(string(ex)), " with ", vals)
        $(esc(f))(vals...)
    end
end
a = 3
r = @logcall max(a, 2a + 1)
println("result ", r)
@logcall a + 1
@logcall 42
examples.output:
call max(a, 2a + 1) with (3, 7)
result 7
call a + 1 with (3, 1)
ERROR: @logcall expects a function call, got 42
  @ @logcall at line 2

sections.title: Small useful macros

sections.body:
A macro is harder to read, to debug and to compose than a function, so use a
function whenever the *values* are all you need. A macro that pastes its
argument twice also **evaluates it twice**, with every side effect: below,
`@square(next!())` calls `next!` twice and multiplies two different numbers,
while the function `square` evaluates its argument once. Julia's compiler
already inlines small functions, so a macro is never needed "for speed".

examples.code:
macro square(ex)
    return :($(esc(ex)) * $(esc(ex)))
end
square(x) = x * x
counter = 0
next!() = (global counter += 1; counter)
println(@square(next!()), " after ", counter, " calls")
counter = 0
println(square(next!()), " after ", counter, " call")
examples.output:
2 after 2 calls
1 after 1 call

sections.title: When a function is enough

sections.body:
`@eval expr` is `eval(:(expr))` with interpolation: a loop over symbols can
define many similar methods at once. This is how Base defines arithmetic for
its many number types, and it is the right tool when the methods differ only
in a name or an operator. The loop runs once, at load time; the generated
methods are ordinary compiled methods, with no run-time cost.

problems.title: A Collatz iterator

sections.body:
Julia has no `interface` keyword. An interface is a documented list of methods
(see [Interfaces](https://docs.julialang.org/en/v1/manual/interfaces/) in the
manual): implement them for your type and every generic function written
against the interface works with it.

The **iteration** interface is the smallest. `for x in itr` is rewritten to

```julia
next = iterate(itr)
while next !== nothing
    (x, state) = next
    # loop body
    next = iterate(itr, state)
end
```

so you define `Base.iterate(itr)` and `Base.iterate(itr, state)`, each
returning `(item, next_state)` or `nothing` at the end. Optional methods tell
generic code more: `Base.length` (and `Base.IteratorSize` when the length is
unknown), and `Base.eltype` so that `collect` can allocate the right array.
Then `collect`, `sum`, `maximum`, comprehensions, `first(itr, n)`, `zip`, …
all work.

examples.code:
struct Countdown
    from::Int
end
Base.iterate(c::Countdown, n = c.from) = n < 1 ? nothing : (n, n - 1)
Base.length(c::Countdown) = max(c.from, 0)
Base.eltype(::Type{Countdown}) = Int

for k in Countdown(3)
    print(k, " ")
end
println()
println(collect(Countdown(4)), " ", sum(Countdown(10)), " ", maximum(Countdown(5)))
println([2k for k in Countdown(3)], " ", first(Countdown(9), 2), " ", collect(zip(Countdown(2), "ab")))

sections.title: Informal interfaces: iteration

sections.body:
Subtype `AbstractArray{T,N}` (or `AbstractVector{T}`, `AbstractMatrix{T}`)
and define two methods:

* `Base.size(A)`: a tuple of dimensions;
* `Base.getindex(A, i::Int)` for a vector, or `getindex(A, i::Int, j::Int, …)`
  with one index per dimension.

That is enough for display, iteration, `sum`, broadcasting, `findfirst`,
slicing, comparisons with `==`, and most of LinearAlgebra. Optional extras:
`Base.setindex!` for a mutable array, and `Base.IndexStyle(::Type{<:MyArray})
= IndexLinear()` when one linear index is the natural way to address the
elements (then you define `getindex(A, i::Int)` even for a matrix). Lazy arrays
compute elements on demand: below, a one-hot vector stores two integers
instead of `n` values, and a multiplication table stores one.

Check the index yourself in `getindex`: `@boundscheck checkbounds(A, i)` raises
a `BoundsError` and lets a caller's `@inbounds` remove the check.

examples.code:
struct OneHot <: AbstractVector{Bool}
    n::Int
    k::Int
end
Base.size(v::OneHot) = (v.n,)
function Base.getindex(v::OneHot, i::Int)
    @boundscheck checkbounds(v, i)
    return i == v.k
end

v = OneHot(5, 2)
println(sum(v), " ", findfirst(v), " ", v == [false, true, false, false, false])
println(v .* 10, " ", [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]' * v)
v
examples.output:
1 2 true
[0, 10, 0, 0, 0] 2
5-element OneHot:
 0
 1
 0
 0
 0

examples.caption: Out-of-range indices are caught by the `checkbounds` we wrote.
examples.code:
struct OneHot <: AbstractVector{Bool}
    n::Int
    k::Int
end
Base.size(v::OneHot) = (v.n,)
function Base.getindex(v::OneHot, i::Int)
    @boundscheck checkbounds(v, i)
    return i == v.k
end
try
    OneHot(5, 2)[7]
catch err
    println(sprint(showerror, err))
end
examples.output: BoundsError: attempt to access 5-element OneHot at index [7]

examples.caption: A lazy matrix with linear indexing: slicing, `sum` and broadcasting come for free.
examples.code:
struct Times <: AbstractMatrix{Int}
    n::Int
end
Base.size(t::Times) = (t.n, t.n)
Base.IndexStyle(::Type{Times}) = IndexLinear()
function Base.getindex(t::Times, i::Int)
    @boundscheck checkbounds(t, i)
    col, row = fldmod1(i, t.n)    # column-major: column = fld1(i, n), row = mod1(i, n)
    return row * col
end

t = Times(4)
println(t[2, 3], " ", sum(t), " ", t[:, 2], " ", typeof(t .+ 1))
t

sections.title: The AbstractArray interface

sections.body:
Two methods control how a value is printed:

* `Base.show(io::IO, x::T)`: the **compact**, one-line form used by `print`,
  `string`, `repr`, string interpolation and inside containers. Ideally it
  looks like code that would recreate the value.
* `Base.show(io::IO, ::MIME"text/plain", x::T)`: the **rich** form the REPL
  (and this site) uses to display a value on its own. It may span several
  lines. If you define only the first, it is used for both.

Do not overload `print` or `display` for this; `show` is the interface they
both call. `get(io, :compact, false)` tells you when the caller asked for an
especially short form (e.g. inside a matrix).

examples.code:
struct Money
    cents::Int
    currency::String
end
amount(m::Money) = string(m.cents ÷ 100, ".", lpad(m.cents % 100, 2, '0'))
Base.show(io::IO, m::Money) = print(io, m.currency, " ", amount(m))
Base.show(io::IO, ::MIME"text/plain", m::Money) =
    print(io, "Money: ", amount(m), " ", m.currency, " (", m.cents, " cents)")

m = Money(1999, "EUR")
println(m)
println([m, Money(5, "EUR")])
println(repr(m), " | ", "price: $m")
m
examples.output:
EUR 19.99
Money[EUR 19.99, EUR 0.05]
EUR 19.99 | price: EUR 19.99
Money: 19.99 EUR (1999 cents)

sections.title: Custom display: show

sections.body:
**Ordering**: define `Base.isless(a::T, b::T)` and `sort`, `sort!`,
`maximum`, `minimum`, `extrema`, `searchsorted` and `<` all work, because
they are written in terms of `isless`. Comparing tuples lexicographically is
a short way to get it right for several fields.

**AbstractDict**: subtype `AbstractDict{K,V}` and define `Base.get(d, k,
default)`, `Base.iterate` and `Base.length`; then `d[k]`, `haskey`, `keys`,
`values`, `pairs` and display work. Below, a read-only dictionary of HTTP
headers that ignores the case of its keys.

examples.code:
struct Version
    major::Int
    minor::Int
    patch::Int
end
Base.isless(a::Version, b::Version) = isless((a.major, a.minor, a.patch), (b.major, b.minor, b.patch))
Base.show(io::IO, v::Version) = print(io, "v", v.major, ".", v.minor, ".", v.patch)

vs = [Version(1, 2, 0), Version(1, 10, 1), Version(0, 9, 9)]
println(sort(vs), " ", maximum(vs), " ", Version(1, 2, 0) < Version(1, 10, 0))

struct Headers <: AbstractDict{String,String}
    data::Dict{String,String}
end
Headers(ps::Pair{String,String}...) = Headers(Dict(lowercase(k) => v for (k, v) in ps))
Base.get(h::Headers, k::AbstractString, default) = get(h.data, lowercase(k), default)
Base.iterate(h::Headers, state...) = iterate(h.data, state...)
Base.length(h::Headers) = length(h.data)

h = Headers("Content-Type" => "text/html", "Accept" => "*/*")
println(h["ACCEPT"], " ", haskey(h, "content-type"), " ", get(h, "X-Missing", "none"), " ", length(h))
h["Cookie"]
examples.output:
*/* true none 2
ERROR: KeyError: key "Cookie" not found
  @ top-level scope at line 11

An informal interface is often implemented half-way, so test it. The `Test`
standard library provides `@test expr` (passes when `expr` is `true`) and
`@test_throws ExceptionType expr`; `@testset "name" begin ... end` groups
tests and prints a summary. Test the *generic* functions that your methods are
supposed to enable, not only the methods themselves: that is what the
interface promises.

A `@test` outside a test set prints `Test Passed`, or the failing expression
with its evaluated values and then throws an error (inside a test set,
failures are counted instead and reported in the summary). A test set prints one summary line with the counts
and the time taken (so that example's output is recorded, not checked).

using Test
@test sum(1:4) == 10
examples.output: Test Passed

A `for x in ch` loop in the consumer stops by itself once the producer is done; keep a running total of `x^2`.

that `put!`s every element of `xs` into a channel, then consume the channel in
the calling function, adding up the squares of the values. Return the total
(an `Int`, `0` for an empty vector).

```julia
channel_square_sum([1, 2, 3])   # 14
```

The grader compares results and measures speed: look at what it says about
the channel's element type and buffer size.

hints: `Iterators.partition(eachindex(xs), len)` gives ranges of indices; `cld(a, b)` is division rounded up.
Collect the tasks in a vector and `fetch` each one; make sure `len` is never 0 when `xs` is empty.
problems.prompt:
Write `parallel_sum(xs, ntasks)` for a `Vector{Int}` `xs` and a positive
`ntasks`. Split the indices of `xs` into (at most) `ntasks` contiguous chunks,
start one `Threads.@spawn` task per chunk that sums its chunk, and add up the
partial sums. Return an `Int`; an empty vector sums to `0`.

```julia
parallel_sum([1, 2, 3, 4, 5], 2)   # 15
parallel_sum(Int[], 4)             # 0
```

This problem is graded on **4 threads**, and every test case runs 10 times:
a shared counter updated by every task gives a different, wrong total from
run to run, and the grader reports it as a data race. Use per-task partial
results. It also measures speed, so see what it says about atomics, locks and

problems.title: A race-free parallel sum

sections.body:
A **task** (also called a coroutine or green thread) is a piece of work that
can be paused and resumed. `@async expr` wraps `expr` in a `Task`, schedules
it, and returns the task immediately, without waiting. `fetch(t)` waits for
the task to finish and returns its value; `wait(t)` waits without returning the
value; `istaskdone(t)` asks whether it has finished.

A task only runs when the current one *yields*: when it waits (`fetch`,
`wait`, `sleep`, I/O, `take!` on an empty channel) or calls `yield()`. Notice
in the first example that the task is not done when we first ask: it has not
even had a chance to start yet.

examples.code:
t = @async begin
    sleep(0.01)
    21 * 2
end
println(istaskdone(t))
println(fetch(t))
println(istaskdone(t))
examples.output:
false
42
true

examples.caption: `@async` is shorthand for creating a `Task` and calling `schedule` on it.
examples.code:
t = Task(() -> println("hello from inside the task"))
println(istaskstarted(t))   # created, but not scheduled yet
schedule(t)
wait(t)
println(istaskdone(t))
examples.output:
false
hello from inside the task
true

examples.caption: Tasks finish in any order, but `fetch` in a fixed order gives a deterministic result. Here the last task finishes first.
examples.code:
tasks = [@async (sleep(0.01 * (4 - i)); i^2) for i in 1:3]
fetch.(tasks)
examples.output:
3-element Vector{Int64}:
 1
 4
 9

examples.caption: An error inside a task surfaces when you `fetch` it, wrapped in a `TaskFailedException`.
examples.code:
t = @async error("boom")
try
    fetch(t)
catch e
    println(typeof(e))
    println(e.task.exception)
end
examples.output:
TaskFailedException
ErrorException("boom")

sections.title: Tasks: start now, collect the result later

sections.body:
A `Channel{T}(n)` is a first-in first-out queue that tasks share: `put!(ch, x)`
adds a value, `take!(ch)` removes the oldest one. The number `n` is the buffer
size: `put!` waits when the buffer is full and `take!` waits when it is empty,
which is what lets a fast producer and a slow consumer cooperate. Give the
channel an element type, as with arrays: `Channel(n)` alone is a
`Channel{Any}`, and every value taken out of it has the abstract type `Any`.

`Channel{T}(f, n)` (usually written with `do`) starts a task running `f(ch)`
and **closes** the channel when `f` returns. A `for` loop over a channel takes
values until the channel is closed and empty, so producer/consumer code needs
no explicit end-of-data marker.

examples.code:
ch = Channel{Int}(3)
put!(ch, 10)
put!(ch, 20)
println(take!(ch))
println(isready(ch))   # is there a value waiting?
println(take!(ch))
println(isready(ch))
examples.output:
10
true
20
false

examples.caption: A producer task; the consumer is the `collect` (or any `for` loop).
examples.code:
squares = Channel{Int}(4) do ch
    for i in 1:5
        put!(ch, i^2)
    end
end   # the channel closes when the do-block returns
collect(squares)
examples.output:
5-element Vector{Int64}:
  1
  4
  9
 16
 25

examples.caption: A two-stage pipeline: each stage is a task reading one channel and writing the next. Values keep their order.
examples.code:
numbers = Channel{Int}(8) do ch
    foreach(i -> put!(ch, i), 1:6)
end
doubled = Channel{Int}(8) do ch
    for x in numbers
        put!(ch, 2x)
    end
end
total = 0
for y in doubled
    global total += y
end
total

examples.caption: Writing to a closed channel is an error.
examples.code:
ch = Channel{Int}(1)
close(ch)
put!(ch, 1)
examples.output:
ERROR: InvalidStateException: Channel is closed.
  @ top-level scope at line 3

sections.title: Channels: passing values between tasks

sections.body:
Everything so far ran on **one** CPU core: the tasks took turns. That is
*concurrency*, and it is what you want for waiting on many things at once
(downloads, files, user input). *Parallelism* means running at the same
moment on several cores, which speeds up computation.

`Threads.@spawn expr` is like `@async` but lets the scheduler run the task on
any of Julia's threads. How many threads there are is fixed when Julia
starts: `julia -t auto` uses one per CPU core, `julia -t 4` uses four (or set
the environment variable `JULIA_NUM_THREADS`). This site runs your code with
**one thread**, so the spawned tasks below take turns, but the same code runs
in parallel when you start Julia with `-t auto` on your own machine, and it
gives the same answer because results are combined only through `fetch`.
(The practice problem at the end of this unit is graded on four threads.)

examples.code: Threads.nthreads()

examples.caption: Split the work into chunks, spawn a task per chunk, add up the partial results.

sections.title: Concurrency is not parallelism: threads

sections.body:
A **data race** happens when tasks update shared state with a read, then a
write, and another task gets in between. `total[] += 1` is exactly that: read
`total[]`, add 1, write it back. With several threads, two tasks can read the
same old value and one increment is lost, so the result changes from run to
run.

On one thread the tasks only switch at yield points, so the race stays hidden.
The example below makes it visible anyway by yielding between the read and
the write: four tasks each add 1 a thousand times, and the total is 1000, not
4000. (With real threads the lost updates happen without any `yield`.)

Three race-free fixes, from best to worst for speed:

* **Per-task partial results**, combined at the end with `fetch` (the
  `chunked_sum` above). No shared state at all.
* **`Threads.Atomic{Int}`** with `Threads.atomic_add!`: the read-modify-write
  becomes one indivisible hardware operation. Works for plain numbers only.
* **A lock** (`ReentrantLock`), held during the whole read-modify-write with
  `lock(l) do ... end`. Works for anything (a `Dict`, a `push!`), but tasks
  queue up to take turns.

examples.caption: A race made visible on one thread: lost updates.
examples.code:
total = Ref(0)
@sync for i in 1:4
    Threads.@spawn for _ in 1:1000
        t = total[]
        yield()            # another task runs between the read and the write
        total[] = t + 1
    end
end
total[]

examples.caption: The same loop with the read-modify-write inside a lock.
examples.code:
total = Ref(0)
l = ReentrantLock()
@sync for i in 1:4
    Threads.@spawn for _ in 1:1000
        lock(l) do
            t = total[]
            yield()
            total[] = t + 1
        end
    end
end
total[]

examples.caption: An atomic counter: `atomic_add!` returns the old value and adds in one step.
examples.code:
total = Threads.Atomic{Int}(0)
@sync for i in 1:4
    Threads.@spawn for _ in 1:1000
        Threads.atomic_add!(total, 1)
    end
end
total[]

sections.title: Data races and how to avoid them

sections.body:
Threads share memory inside one Julia process. Two other kinds of parallelism
are worth knowing about (Distributed ships with Julia and unit 40 starts a worker
with it; no GPU package is installed in this sandbox):

* **Distributed** (a standard library): `addprocs(4)` starts worker
  *processes*, possibly on other machines; `@everywhere` defines code on all of
  them, and `pmap(f, xs)` or `@distributed` share out the work. Workers do not
  share memory, so data is copied to them: worth it for large independent jobs.
* **GPUs**: packages such as CUDA.jl (NVIDIA), AMDGPU.jl and Metal.jl (Apple)
  provide array types that live on the graphics card. Broadcasting and many
  array functions on them run as GPU kernels, and you can write your own
  kernels in Julia.

Whatever the hardware, the rules from this unit carry over: split the work so
that each worker owns its piece, and combine the results at the end.
sections.title: Beyond one process: Distributed and GPUs

hints: `Base.return_types(f, argtypes)` returns a vector of inferred return types, one per matching method.
The vector can be empty; `isconcretetype(T)` is false for `Any` and for a `Union` of two types.
problems.prompt:
Write `infers_concretely(f, argtypes)`, where `argtypes` is a tuple of types
such as `(Int,)` or `(Int, Float64)`. Return `true` when type inference finds
exactly one, concrete, return type for calling `f` with arguments of those
types, and `false` otherwise (an abstract type, a `Union`, or no matching
method at all).


problems.title: Ask the compiler: is the return type concrete?

sections.body:
When you call a function, Julia picks the **method** by the types of all the
arguments (multiple dispatch), and then compiles that method for exactly those
argument types. The compiled version is a **method instance** (a
*specialization*). `double(x) = 2x` is one method, but calling it with an
`Int` and with a `Float64` compiles two separate pieces of machine code, each
as fast as if you had written it for that type by hand.

`methods(f)` lists the methods; `Base.specializations(m)` lists the instances
compiled for method `m` so far (we sort them by name, because the order they
are stored in is not meaningful). `Base.return_types(f, (T,))` asks type
inference what the result type would be for argument type `T`, without
running anything.

examples.code:
double(x) = 2x
double(3)
double(2.5)
println(methods(double))
m = only(methods(double))
sort([string(mi) for mi in Base.specializations(m)])
examples.output:
# 1 method for generic function "double" from Main:
 [1] double(x)
     @ main.jl:1
2-element Vector{String}:
 "MethodInstance for double(::Float64)"
 "MethodInstance for double(::Int64)"

examples.caption: Inference works per argument type: one return type for each.
examples.code:
double(x) = 2x
println(Base.return_types(double, (Int,)))
println(Base.return_types(double, (Float64,)))
println(Base.return_types(double, (Rational{Int},)))
examples.output:
Any[Int64]
Any[Float64]
Any[Rational{Int64}]

examples.caption: A function whose return type depends on a *value* is type-unstable: inference can only say `Union{Float64, Int64}`.
examples.code:
pos(x) = x > 0 ? x : 0.0
Base.return_types(pos, (Int,))
examples.output:
1-element Vector{Any}:
 Union{Float64, Int64}

sections.title: One method, many specializations

sections.body:
`@code_typed f(args...)` shows the code after type inference and
optimization: each line is one operation with its inferred type after `::`,
and `=> T` at the end is the return type. The `@code_...` macros live in the
`InteractiveUtils` standard library, which the REPL loads for you; in a
script (and on this site) write `using InteractiveUtils` first.

Notice what is *not* there: `2x` for an `Int` became a single
`Base.mul_int` (an integer multiplication), with no dispatch left at run time.
In the unstable `pos`, the two `return` lines have different types; that is
what `@code_warntype` highlights in red at the REPL.

One level further down, `@code_llvm` shows LLVM's intermediate code and
`@code_native` the machine instructions. Their output depends on your CPU
and contains generated names that change between runs, so we only show one
example, unchecked.

examples.output:
CodeInfo(
1 ─ %1 = Base.mul_int(2, x)::Int64
└──      return %1
) => Int64

examples.caption: Unchecked: the function name in the first line (`julia_double_…`) carries a counter that varies between runs.

sections.title: Reading the compiled code: @code_typed

sections.body:
Two optimizations explain a lot of Julia's speed:

* **Inlining**: a small function's body is pasted into its caller, so the
  call disappears. `x^3` with a literal exponent is turned into two
  multiplications this way.
* **Constant propagation**: when arguments are known constants, inference
  computes with the values, not just the types. Below, `answer()` calls
  `inc(41)`; the optimized code is just `return 42`.

`optimize = false` shows the code before these passes: the call to `inc` is
still there, but inference already knows its result is the constant 42
(`Core.Const(42)`).

examples.code:
using InteractiveUtils
inc(x) = x + 1
answer() = inc(41)
@code_typed answer()

using InteractiveUtils
inc(x) = x + 1
answer() = inc(41)
@code_typed optimize = false answer()
examples.output:
CodeInfo(
1 ─ %1 = Main.inc(41)::Core.Const(42)
└──      return %1
) => Int64

examples.caption: A literal power is inlined into plain multiplications.
examples.output:
CodeInfo(
1 ─ %1 = Base.mul_int(x, x)::Int64
│   %2 = Base.mul_int(%1, x)::Int64
└──      return %2
) => Int64

sections.title: Constant propagation and inlining

sections.body:
Every method definition increments a global counter, the **world age**. A
running function sees the methods that existed in the world where it
started, so the compiled code it is running stays valid. If a function
defines a new method with `@eval` (or `include`) and calls it right away, the
call fails with "method too new to be called from this world context".

`Base.invokelatest(f, args...)` makes the call in the newest world. It is
slower (a dynamic call), so use it at the boundary where code is loaded, not
in an inner loop. At the top level of a script or the REPL each statement
starts in the latest world, which is why this never bites there.

The two world ages in the message are large numbers that depend on how many
methods were defined before, so the course shows them as `W` and `W+1`.

examples.code:
function load_and_call()
    @eval plugin() = "plugin loaded"
    try
        plugin()
    catch e
        println(typeof(e))
    end
    println(Base.invokelatest(plugin))
end
load_and_call()
println(plugin())   # top level: the latest world again
examples.output:
MethodError
plugin loaded
plugin loaded

examples.caption: The MethodError says exactly this.
examples.output:
ERROR: MethodError: no method matching newfun()
The applicable method may be too new: running in world age W, while current world is W+1.

Closest candidates are:
  newfun() (method too new to be called from this world context.)
   @ Main main.jl:2

  @ define_and_call at line 3
  @ top-level scope at line 5

sections.title: World age: why eval'd methods need invokelatest

sections.body:
Compilation happens the first time each method instance is called, so the
first call is slow and later ones are fast. This is the "time to first x"
(TTFX) you notice when a package's first plot takes seconds. The example
below is unchecked because it prints timings; `@time` reports the share of
compilation time on the first call.

To cut that cost, packages **precompile**: when you install or update one,
Julia stores its compiled code in a cache file (`.ji` plus, since Julia
1.9, native code in a `.so`/`.dll`) so later sessions can load it.
Precompilation workloads (PrecompileTools.jl's `@compile_workload`) run
typical calls at that time so their specializations are cached too.

An **invalidation** happens when a newly loaded method could change what
existing compiled code would call: Julia must throw that code away and
compile it again. Defining `Base.+` for a new combination of Base types (type
piracy) is a classic cause. SnoopCompile.jl finds invalidations and
inference bottlenecks when load times matter.

examples.output:
0.079154 seconds (28.34 k allocations: 1.951 MiB, 99.96% compilation time)
  0.000010 seconds (1 allocation: 16 bytes)
0.3384236261145569

hints: Compute the mean and the standard deviation once, before the element-wise step.
A single dotted expression such as `(v .- m) ./ s` fuses into one loop that fills one new array.
problems.prompt:
Write `zscore(v)` that returns a new vector holding the z-score of every
element of the `Vector{Float64}` `v`: `(v[i] - mean(v)) / std(v)`, with the
sample standard deviation as `std` computes it. Do not change `v`. Assume
`length(v) ≥ 2`.

sections.body:
The **standard library** is a set of packages that come with Julia: you load
them with `using` but never install them. `LinearAlgebra` adds `norm`, `dot`,
`det`, `eigen`, factorizations, and `I`, the identity of whatever size is
needed. Matrix literals separate columns with spaces and rows with `;`, and
`*` on matrices is the matrix product (`.*` is element by element).

To solve `A x = b`, write `A \ b`. It picks a suitable factorization (LU for
a square matrix, QR for a tall one, which gives the least-squares solution)
and is both faster and more accurate than `inv(A) * b`.

Floating-point results from the underlying BLAS/LAPACK libraries can differ
in the last digits between machines, so the examples round them with
`round.(x; digits = 6)`.

examples.code:
using LinearAlgebra
A = [4.0 1.0; 1.0 3.0]
b = [1.0, 2.0]
x = A \ b
println(round.(x; digits = 6))
println(A * x ≈ b)                        # ≈ compares with a tolerance
println(round(det(A); digits = 6), " ", round(norm([3.0, 4.0]); digits = 6), " ", dot([1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]))

examples.caption: `I` adapts its size to the matrix it is added to.
examples.code:
using LinearAlgebra
A = [4.0 1.0; 1.0 3.0]
A + 2I

examples.caption: Eigenvalues of a symmetric matrix (wrapping it in `Symmetric` selects the symmetric solver; the values come out sorted).
examples.code:
using LinearAlgebra
S = Symmetric([2.0 1.0; 1.0 2.0])
E = eigen(S)
λ = round.(E.values; digits = 6)
v = E.vectors[:, 2]
println(λ)
println(round(norm(S * v - E.values[2] * v); digits = 12))

examples.caption: `SparseArrays` stores only the non-zero entries (shown as `⋅`): useful for large matrices that are mostly zeros.
examples.code:
using SparseArrays
S = sparse([1, 2, 3, 3], [1, 2, 3, 1], [10.0, 20.0, 30.0, 5.0])
println(nnz(S), " stored entries")
S

4 stored entries
3×3 SparseMatrixCSC{Float64, Int64} with 4 stored entries:
 10.0    ⋅     ⋅

sections.body:
`Statistics` provides `mean`, `median`, `var`, `std`, `quantile` and `cor`.
Two defaults to know:

* `var` and `std` are the **sample** versions (divide by n − 1), like R and
  unlike NumPy's default; pass `corrected = false` to divide by n.
* `quantile` uses the same default definition as R (type 7, linear
  interpolation between order statistics).

examples.code:
using Statistics
x = [2.0, 4.0, 4.0, 4.0, 5.0, 5.0, 7.0, 9.0]
println(mean(x), " ", median(x))
println(round(var(x); digits = 6), " ", round(std(x); digits = 6))
println(var(x; corrected = false), " ", std(x; corrected = false))
println(quantile(x, [0.25, 0.75]))

examples.caption: Pearson correlation; `mean` over the columns of a matrix with `dims`.
examples.code:
using Statistics
println(round(cor([1, 2, 3, 4], [2, 4, 5, 9]); digits = 6))
M = [1 2; 3 4; 5 6]
mean(M; dims = 1)

sections.body:
For reproducible results, create a random number generator with a seed and
pass it as the first argument: `rand(rng, ...)`, `randn(rng, ...)`,
`shuffle(rng, v)`, `randperm(rng, n)`. The same seed gives the same
sequence. `Xoshiro` is Julia's default generator.

Be aware that the numbers a given seed produces may change between Julia
versions (they are only guaranteed within a release). For data that must stay
the same forever, such as test fixtures, use a package like StableRNGs.jl.
Functions that need randomness should take the generator as an argument, so
callers (and tests) can control it.

examples.code:
using Random
rng = Xoshiro(1234)
println(rand(rng, 1:6, 5))      # five dice rolls
println(rand(rng, 1:6, 5))      # the generator moved on: different rolls
println(rand(Xoshiro(1234), 1:6, 5) == rand(Xoshiro(1234), 1:6, 5))

using Random
rng = Xoshiro(7)
println(shuffle(rng, 1:6))
println(randperm(rng, 6))
println(round.(randn(rng, 3); digits = 4))

sections.body:
`Date` is a calendar day, `DateTime` a day plus a time to the millisecond.
Arithmetic uses *periods* such as `Day(1)`, `Month(1)`, `Hour(12)`;
subtracting two dates gives a number of days. `dayofweek` numbers days from
Monday = 1 to Sunday = 7. A range of dates, `d1:Day(1):d2`, iterates over
every day in between.

`Date("2024-12-25")` parses ISO dates; for other layouts give a format,
written with the `dateformat"..."` string macro so it is parsed only once:
`y` year, `m` month number, `u` abbreviated month name, `d` day, `H` hours,
`M` minutes.

examples.code:
using Dates
d = Date(2024, 2, 28)
println(d + Day(1), " ", d + Day(2))     # 2024 is a leap year
println(Date(2024, 3, 1) - d)
println(dayofweek(d), " ", dayname(d))
println(d + Month(1))

using Dates
dt = DateTime(2024, 3, 10, 14, 30)
println(dt + Hour(12))
println(Dates.format(dt, dateformat"dd u yyyy, HH:MM"))
println(Date("25/12/2024", dateformat"dd/mm/yyyy"))

examples.caption: Count the Saturdays in March 2024 with a range of dates.
examples.code:
using Dates
march = Date(2024, 3, 1):Day(1):Date(2024, 3, 31)
count(d -> dayofweek(d) == Saturday, march)

sections.body:
`@printf` and `@sprintf` (from `Printf`) format numbers C-style: `%.3f`
three decimals, `%5d` an integer padded to width 5, `%-6s` a left-aligned
string, `%e` scientific notation, `%08.2f` zero padding. The format is
checked when the macro expands.

`Test` is how Julia packages are tested. `@test expr` passes when `expr` is
`true`; `@test a ≈ b` compares floats with a tolerance (never use `==` on
computed floats); `@test_throws T expr` passes when `expr` throws a `T`.
`@testset` groups tests and prints a summary. The summary normally has a
`Time` column; `showtiming = false` removes it, which we need here so the
output is the same on every run. A failing `@test` outside a testset is an
error that shows the expression and its evaluated value.

examples.code:
using Printf
@printf("%.3f|%5d|%-6s|%e\n", pi, 42, "ab", 12345.678)
s = @sprintf("%08.2f", 3.14159)
s

examples.output:
Test Summary: | Pass  Total  
arithmetic    |    3      3

using Test
@test 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3
