  conditions at a solver's answer").

Every facility-location example uses the same data from `StableRNG(2024)`.
Relaxation bounds and optimal values are deterministic (an LP's optimal
value is unique even when its solution is not); node counts and times are
not, so no example shows them.
sections.title: What you need from earlier units

sections.body:
**Uncapacitated facility location**: open some of 8 facilities (binary
`y_j`, fixed cost `f_j`) and serve each of 30 customers from open ones
(`x_ij ≥ 0`, the fraction of customer `i` served by `j`, cost `c_ij`):

    min  Σ f_j y_j + Σ c_ij x_ij
    s.t. Σ_j x_ij = 1               every customer is served
         x_ij can be > 0 only if y_j = 1

The last line must become linear constraints, and there are two classic
ways, with **the same integer solutions**:

* **aggregated**: `Σ_i x_ij ≤ 30 y_j` (one constraint per facility);
* **disaggregated**: `x_ij ≤ y_j` (one per pair).

Their LP relaxations differ. A fractional `y_j = 0.1` lets a facility serve
three whole customers in the aggregated form but only a tenth of each in
the disaggregated one. The relaxation of the disaggregated form is
**tighter** (its feasible set is smaller), so its bound is higher, closer
to the integer optimum, and branch and bound prunes more. On this instance
its bound equals the integer optimum, so there is no gap left for branch
and bound to close.

examples.caption: Facility location (8 facilities, 30 customers, `StableRNG(2024)`) in the two formulations: the LP relaxation bound (`relax_integrality`) and the integer optimum, rounded to 4 digits.
examples.code:
using JuMP, HiGHS, StableRNGs
rng = StableRNG(2024)
nf, nc = 8, 30
fx, fy, cx, cy = rand(rng, nf), rand(rng, nf), rand(rng, nc), rand(rng, nc)
cost = [10 * hypot(cx[i] - fx[j], cy[i] - fy[j]) for i in 1:nc, j in 1:nf]
fixed = 3.0 .+ rand(rng, nf)
function facility(form; relax = false)
    model = Model(HiGHS.Optimizer)
    set_silent(model)
    set_attribute(model, "mip_rel_gap", 0.0)
    @variable(model, y[1:nf], Bin)
    @variable(model, 0 <= x[1:nc, 1:nf] <= 1)
    @constraint(model, [i in 1:nc], sum(x[i, :]) == 1)
    if form == :aggregated
        @constraint(model, [j in 1:nf], sum(x[:, j]) <= nc * y[j])
    else
        @constraint(model, [i in 1:nc, j in 1:nf], x[i, j] <= y[j])
    end
    @objective(model, Min, sum(fixed .* y) + sum(cost .* x))
    relax && relax_integrality(model)
    optimize!(model)
    return model
end
for form in (:aggregated, :disaggregated)
    lp, mip = facility(form; relax = true), facility(form)
    println(rpad(form, 14), " LP bound ", rpad(round(objective_value(lp); digits = 4), 8), " integer optimum ",
            round(objective_value(mip); digits = 4), "  open ", findall(round.(Int, value.(mip[:y])) .== 1))
end
examples.notice: Notice that both formulations reach the same integer optimum, 81.1509, with the same open facilities, while their relaxation bounds are 65.05 and 81.15: the aggregated form leaves a gap of 20% for branch and bound to close, the disaggregated form none.
examples.output:
aggregated     LP bound 65.0506  integer optimum 81.1509  open [1, 2, 4, 6, 8]
disaggregated  LP bound 81.1509  integer optimum 81.1509  open [1, 2, 4, 6, 8]

choices: The one with bound 65, since its relaxation is easier to solve
The one with bound 81, since it prunes branches sooner
Neither: the same integer solutions give the same search tree
questions.explain: A node is pruned when its bound reaches the best known integer value. With the tighter formulation the root bound already equals the optimum, so every branch is pruned as soon as an optimal solution is found; with bound 65, the solver must branch until it has raised the bound by 16.
misconceptions: Each relaxation is an LP of similar size; what costs time in branch and bound is the number of nodes, which the bound controls.
The search depends on the relaxations at each node, and those differ between formulations even when the integer points are the same.
questions.prompt: Two formulations of the same minimization problem have the same integer solutions. One has LP relaxation bound 65, the other 81, and the integer optimum is 81. Which do you expect branch and bound to solve with fewer nodes?

sections.title: The LP relaxation, and why formulations differ

sections.body:
A **big-M** constraint switches a constraint off with a binary: for
`x_ij ≤ M y_j`, `y_j = 1` gives `x_ij ≤ M`, which must not cut off any
feasible `x_ij`, and `y_j = 0` gives `x_ij ≤ 0`. So `M` must be at least
the largest value `x_ij` can take; here the bounds `0 ≤ x_ij ≤ 1` make
`M = 1` valid and also the **tightest** valid value.

The general rule: to make `a'x ≤ b` hold only when `z = 1`, write
`a'x ≤ b + M (1 - z)` with

    M = max over the domain of (a'x - b)

which for box bounds `lo ≤ x ≤ hi` is `Σ_i max(a_i lo_i, a_i hi_i) - b`
(each term takes the bound that makes `a_i x_i` largest). A larger `M` is
still valid but weakens the relaxation: with `y_j = x_ij / M` the
relaxation pays only a fraction `1/M` of the fixed cost. Big-M with the
tightest `M = 1` is the disaggregated formulation of the last section.

The [JuMP tips and tricks](https://jump.dev/JuMP.jl/stable/tutorials/linear/tips_and_tricks/)
page gives the advice in one line: "Try to use domain knowledge to choose
an `M` that is just right", and warns about both directions, which the next
two sections show.

examples.caption: The disaggregated model written as `x[i, j] <= M * y[j]` with `M = 1e6`, `100` and `1`: LP bound and integer optimum (rounded to 4 digits).
examples.code:
using JuMP, HiGHS, StableRNGs
rng = StableRNG(2024)
nf, nc = 8, 30
fx, fy, cx, cy = rand(rng, nf), rand(rng, nf), rand(rng, nc), rand(rng, nc)
cost = [10 * hypot(cx[i] - fx[j], cy[i] - fy[j]) for i in 1:nc, j in 1:nf]
fixed = 3.0 .+ rand(rng, nf)
function facility(M; relax = false)
    model = Model(HiGHS.Optimizer)
    set_silent(model)
    set_attribute(model, "mip_rel_gap", 0.0)
    @variable(model, y[1:nf], Bin)
    @variable(model, x[1:nc, 1:nf] >= 0)
    @constraint(model, [i in 1:nc], sum(x[i, :]) == 1)
    @constraint(model, [i in 1:nc, j in 1:nf], x[i, j] <= M * y[j])
    @objective(model, Min, sum(fixed .* y) + sum(cost .* x))
    relax && relax_integrality(model)
    optimize!(model)
    return model
end
for M in (1e6, 100.0, 1.0)
    println("M = ", rpad(M, 6), " LP bound ", rpad(round(objective_value(facility(M; relax = true)); digits = 4), 8),
            " integer optimum ", round(objective_value(facility(M)); digits = 4))
end
println("nearest facility for everyone, no fixed cost: ", round(sum(minimum(cost; dims = 2)); digits = 4))
examples.notice: Notice that with the default presolve all three return the right optimum, 81.1509, but the bound with `M = 1e6` or `100` is 61.65 or 61.90, close to the last line, the cost of serving every customer from its nearest facility with no fixed cost at all: a loose `M` makes the relaxation ignore the fixed costs.
examples.output:
M = 1.0e6  LP bound 61.6512  integer optimum 81.1509
M = 100.0  LP bound 61.895   integer optimum 81.1509
M = 1.0    LP bound 81.1509  integer optimum 81.1509
nearest facility for everyone, no fixed cost: 61.6511

choices: 11, the largest value of `3x₁ - 2x₂ - 4` on the box
31, from the largest `x₁` and the largest `x₂`
1e6, since any large number is safe
15, from the largest value of `3x₁`
questions.explain: With `z = 0` the constraint must allow every point of the box, so `M ≥ max(3x₁ - 2x₂) - 4 = 3·5 - 2·0 - 4 = 11`. Each term takes the bound that makes it largest: `x₁ = 5` for the positive coefficient, `x₂ = 0` for the negative one.
misconceptions: `x₂` has a negative coefficient, so its upper bound makes `3x₁ - 2x₂` smaller, not larger; adding `2 · 10` to the bound double counts in the wrong direction.
A huge `M` is valid but weakens the relaxation and, with the integrality tolerance, can produce wrong answers (next section).
That forgets to subtract the right-hand side 4: the constraint already allows `3x₁ - 2x₂` up to 4 without any `M`.
questions.prompt: To enforce `3x₁ - 2x₂ ≤ 4` only when `z = 1`, with `0 ≤ x₁ ≤ 5` and `0 ≤ x₂ ≤ 10`, you write `3x₁ - 2x₂ ≤ 4 + M(1 - z)`. What is the smallest valid `M`?

sections.title: Sizing big-M from bounds

sections.body:
A MIP solver accepts a value as integer when it is within a tolerance:
HiGHS's `mip_feasibility_tolerance` ("MIP integrality tolerance") defaults
to `1e-6` according to its [options
list](https://ergo-code.github.io/HiGHS/dev/options/definitions/). With
`M = 1e6`, the value `y_j = 1e-6` counts as 0, yet `x_ij ≤ M y_j` then
allows `x_ij ≤ 1`: a facility that is "closed" serves customers in full,
and its fixed cost is paid only a millionth. The solver has found a
solution that is feasible **by its tolerances** and wrong for the model.

In the previous section HiGHS's presolve protected us (presolve can tighten
the coefficients of such rows). With presolve switched off the problem
shows. The JuMP tips page warns: "If `M` is too big, the solver may
encounter numerical issues."

The check is the one from unit 38: take the solver's answer, round the
integer variables, and evaluate the model's constraints yourself.

examples.caption: The `M = 1e6` model with `presolve = "off"`: status, objective, the largest `y_j` that rounds to 0 and how many of those are above 0, and the worst violation of `x[i, j] <= y[j]` after rounding the `y` (rounded to 4 digits).
examples.code:
using JuMP, HiGHS, StableRNGs
rng = StableRNG(2024)
nf, nc = 8, 30
fx, fy, cx, cy = rand(rng, nf), rand(rng, nf), rand(rng, nc), rand(rng, nc)
cost = [10 * hypot(cx[i] - fx[j], cy[i] - fy[j]) for i in 1:nc, j in 1:nf]
fixed = 3.0 .+ rand(rng, nf)
for M in (1e6, 1.0)
    model = Model(HiGHS.Optimizer)
    set_silent(model)
    set_attribute(model, "mip_rel_gap", 0.0)
    set_attribute(model, "presolve", "off")
    @variable(model, y[1:nf], Bin)
    @variable(model, x[1:nc, 1:nf] >= 0)
    @constraint(model, [i in 1:nc], sum(x[i, :]) == 1)
    @constraint(model, [i in 1:nc, j in 1:nf], x[i, j] <= M * y[j])
    @objective(model, Min, sum(fixed .* y) + sum(cost .* x))
    optimize!(model)
    yv, xv = value.(y), value.(x)
    yr = round.(Int, yv)
    closed = [yv[j] for j in 1:nf if yr[j] == 0]
    println("M = ", rpad(M, 6), termination_status(model), ", objective ", round(objective_value(model); digits = 4),
            ", open ", count(==(1), yr), ", largest y rounded to 0: ", isempty(closed) ? "none" : maximum(closed),
            " (", count(>(0), closed), " of them above 0)",
            ", violation after rounding ", round(maximum(xv[i, j] - yr[j] for i in 1:nc, j in 1:nf); digits = 4) + 0.0)
end
examples.notice: Notice that HiGHS reports `OPTIMAL` with objective 61.6512, the relaxation bound, with every facility closed: seven of the eight `y_j` are `1e-6`, exactly the integrality tolerance (the eighth facility serves no one and is 0), and after rounding customers are served by closed facilities in full (violation 1.0). The same model with `M = 1` gives 81.1509 with presolve off too.
examples.output:
M = 1.0e6 OPTIMAL, objective 61.6512, open 0, largest y rounded to 0: 1.0e-6 (7 of them above 0), violation after rounding 1.0
M = 1.0   OPTIMAL, objective 81.1509, open 5, largest y rounded to 0: 0.0 (0 of them above 0), violation after rounding 0.0

choices: Yes: the solver returned `OPTIMAL`, so the constraints hold
No: `z` can be about `1e-6`, which allows `x` up to 10
Yes, since rounding `z` to 0 is how integers are read
questions.explain: `z = 1e-6` passes the integrality test, and `1e7 · 1e-6 = 10`. The solver's model is satisfied within tolerance; yours, with `z` exactly 0, is not. Use the smallest valid `M` and check the rounded solution against the constraints.
misconceptions: `OPTIMAL` means optimal within HiGHS's tolerances; with `M` this large, a tolerance on `z` becomes a large slack on `x`.
Rounding is how to read the answer, but the rounded `z = 0` with `x = 10` violates `x ≤ 1e7 · z`; the solver never had to satisfy that.
questions.prompt: A model has `x ≤ 1e7 · z` with `z` binary and HiGHS's integrality tolerance `1e-6`. The solver reports `z = 0` (after rounding) and `x = 10`. Is that a solution of your model?

sections.title: Too big: the integrality tolerance opens a facility by a millionth

sections.body:
An `M` below the tightest valid value is a different model: it forbids
feasible points. With `x_ij ≤ 0.5 y_j`, no facility can serve a customer
alone, so every customer must be split between two open facilities. The
solver solves this model correctly and reports `OPTIMAL`; nothing in its
output says the model is not the one you meant. The JuMP tips page: "If
`M` is too small, the solution may be suboptimal."

Two checks catch it:

* **Bounds**: compute the tightest `M` from the variables' bounds, as in
  the previous section, and compare.
* **Tight big-M rows**: in the answer, a big-M row `x ≤ M y` that holds
  with equality while `y = 1` means `M` itself is limiting the solution.
  With a valid `M`, such a row is tight only because `x` reached its own
  bound.

examples.caption: The model with `M = 0.5` against `M = 1`: objective, open facilities, and how many rows `x[i, j] <= M y[j]` are tight with `y[j] = 1` (to `1e-6`).
examples.code:
using JuMP, HiGHS, StableRNGs
rng = StableRNG(2024)
nf, nc = 8, 30
fx, fy, cx, cy = rand(rng, nf), rand(rng, nf), rand(rng, nc), rand(rng, nc)
cost = [10 * hypot(cx[i] - fx[j], cy[i] - fy[j]) for i in 1:nc, j in 1:nf]
fixed = 3.0 .+ rand(rng, nf)
for M in (0.5, 1.0)
    model = Model(HiGHS.Optimizer)
    set_silent(model)
    set_attribute(model, "mip_rel_gap", 0.0)
    @variable(model, y[1:nf], Bin)
    @variable(model, x[1:nc, 1:nf] >= 0)
    @constraint(model, [i in 1:nc], sum(x[i, :]) == 1)
    @constraint(model, [i in 1:nc, j in 1:nf], x[i, j] <= M * y[j])
    @objective(model, Min, sum(fixed .* y) + sum(cost .* x))
    optimize!(model)
    yr = round.(Int, value.(y))
    tight = count(yr[j] == 1 && abs(value(x[i, j]) - M) < 1e-6 for i in 1:nc, j in 1:nf)
    println("M = ", M, ": ", termination_status(model), ", objective ", round(objective_value(model); digits = 4),
            ", open ", count(==(1), yr), ", tight big-M rows ", tight)
end
examples.notice: Notice that `M = 0.5` gives a solution 24% more expensive, with six facilities instead of five, reported as `OPTIMAL`, and that 60 big-M rows are tight: every customer is split in halves, pushed against the artificial limit.
examples.output:
M = 0.5: OPTIMAL, objective 100.998, open 6, tight big-M rows 60
M = 1.0: OPTIMAL, objective 81.1509, open 5, tight big-M rows 30

choices: The solution is degenerate, which is common and harmless in LPs
`M` is smaller than the tightest valid value and is cutting off solutions
The integrality tolerance is too loose for the size of `M`
questions.explain: With a valid `M`, `x ≤ M y` can only be tight at `y = 1` if `x` has reached a bound it would have anyway. Equality below `x`'s own bound means `M` is the binding limit: the model is more restrictive than the problem.
misconceptions: Degeneracy is about several active constraints at a vertex; it does not explain why the binding limit is `M` rather than `x`'s bound.
That problem comes from a large `M` and shows up as `y` slightly above 0; here `y = 1` and the limit is `M` itself.
questions.prompt: Your MIP returns `OPTIMAL`, and in the solution many big-M rows `x ≤ M y` with `y = 1` hold with equality, at values of `x` below `x`'s own upper bound. What should you suspect?

sections.title: Too small: a cut-off optimum, reported as optimal

sections.body:
An **indicator constraint** states the logic directly: "if `y_j = 0` then
`x_ij ≤ 0`". JuMP writes it with `-->` (from the tips page):
`@constraint(model, !y[j] --> {x[i, j] <= 0})`, and `y[j] --> {...}`
for "if `y_j = 1`". Some solvers handle indicators natively. HiGHS does
not, so MathOptInterface's `IndicatorToMILPBridge` rewrites each one as a
big-M constraint, computing `M` from the **bounds of the variables**: its
source reads the bounds of the constrained expression and throws
`BridgeRequiresFiniteDomainError` when they are infinite.

So an indicator constraint is not a way around big-M with HiGHS; it is
big-M with `M` computed for you from the bounds you declared. Declare the
tightest bounds you know, and an indicator gives the tightest `M` without
the arithmetic.

examples.caption: The facility model with indicator constraints `!y[j] --> {x[i, j] <= 0}`, first with the bound `x <= 1` declared, then without it.
examples.code:
using JuMP, HiGHS, StableRNGs
rng = StableRNG(2024)
nf, nc = 8, 30
fx, fy, cx, cy = rand(rng, nf), rand(rng, nf), rand(rng, nc), rand(rng, nc)
cost = [10 * hypot(cx[i] - fx[j], cy[i] - fy[j]) for i in 1:nc, j in 1:nf]
fixed = 3.0 .+ rand(rng, nf)
for bounded in (true, false)
    model = Model(HiGHS.Optimizer)
    set_silent(model)
    set_attribute(model, "mip_rel_gap", 0.0)
    @variable(model, y[1:nf], Bin)
    @variable(model, x[1:nc, 1:nf] >= 0)
    bounded && set_upper_bound.(x, 1.0)
    @constraint(model, [i in 1:nc], sum(x[i, :]) == 1)
    @constraint(model, [i in 1:nc, j in 1:nf], !y[j] --> {x[i, j] <= 0})
    @objective(model, Min, sum(fixed .* y) + sum(cost .* x))
    try
        optimize!(model)
        println("x <= 1 declared: ", termination_status(model), ", objective ", round(objective_value(model); digits = 4))
    catch e
        println("no upper bound: ", e isa MOI.Bridges.BridgeRequiresFiniteDomainError ? "BridgeRequiresFiniteDomainError" : typeof(e))
    end
end
examples.notice: Notice that with the bound the indicator model reaches the optimum 81.1509, the same as the tight big-M model, and that without an upper bound on `x` the bridge cannot compute an `M` and refuses the model.
examples.output:
x <= 1 declared: OPTIMAL, objective 81.1509
no upper bound: BridgeRequiresFiniteDomainError

choices: None: HiGHS enforces the logic exactly in its search
1, the smallest value that is always safe
1e6, from the declared upper bound of `x`
questions.explain: HiGHS has no native indicator support, so the bridge builds a big-M row from the bounds it can see, here `x ≤ 1e6`. The indicator saves you the arithmetic, not the modelling: a loose declared bound gives the same loose `M`.
misconceptions: That is what a solver with native indicator support may do; with HiGHS the bridge turns the indicator into a big-M row.
The bridge cannot know the problem allows only `x ≤ 1`; it uses the declared bound, which is 1e6.
questions.prompt: You replace `x ≤ 1e6 · y` by `!y --> {x <= 0}` and solve with HiGHS, with `0 ≤ x ≤ 1e6` declared. What `M` does the reformulation use?

sections.title: Indicator constraints

sections.body:
A product of variables is not linear, but a product with a **binary**
factor can be written exactly with linear constraints.

* **Two binaries**, `z = y₁ y₂`: `z ≤ y₁`, `z ≤ y₂`, `z ≥ y₁ + y₂ - 1`,
  `0 ≤ z ≤ 1`. For binary `y`, these force `z` to the product (the "And"
  rule on the JuMP tips page; `z` itself need not be declared binary).
* **A binary and a bounded continuous variable**, `z = y x` with
  `0 ≤ x ≤ U`: `z ≤ U y`, `z ≤ x`, `z ≥ x - U (1 - y)`, `z ≥ 0`. This is
  big-M again, with `M = U` from the bound.

Only the constraints that can bind are needed: in a maximization where
`z` has a positive coefficient, the solver wants `z` large, so `z ≤ y₁`
and `z ≤ y₂` matter and `z ≥ y₁ + y₂ - 1` never binds; with a negative
coefficient it is the other way round. Writing all of them is safe.

The example selects at most 3 of 6 projects with values `w_i` and pairwise
synergies `P_ij` (some negative, for conflicts), maximizing
`Σ w_i y_i + Σ_{i<j} P_ij y_i y_j`, and checks the linearized model against
enumerating all 64 subsets.

examples.caption: Project selection with pairwise terms, linearized with one `z` per pair, against brute-force enumeration; then the same model without the `z ≥ y_i + y_j - 1` rows.
examples.notice: Notice that the full linearization matches enumeration exactly, and that dropping the lower-bound rows lets the solver set `z = 0` for the conflicting pairs, ignoring their penalty: it picks a set containing the conflict between projects 3 and 5 and reports a higher value, which that set does not achieve.
examples.output:
enumeration: 15.0
linearized:  (15.0, [1, 5, 6])
without z ≥ y_i + y_j - 1: (16.0, [3, 5, 6])

questions.code:
y1, y2 = 1, 1
lo = max(0, y1 + y2 - 1)
hi = min(y1, y2, 1)
(lo, hi)
questions.explain: `z ≥ y₁ + y₂ - 1 = 1` and `z ≤ min(y₁, y₂) = 1`: the interval collapses to `z = 1 = y₁ y₂`. For the other three binary combinations it collapses to 0. That is why `z` can be continuous.
misconceptions: That drops the lower bound `z ≥ y₁ + y₂ - 1`; without it the product is not enforced from below, which is the bug in the last example.
The upper bound is `min(y₁, y₂)`, not `y₁ + y₂`; `z` represents a product of binaries, which is at most 1.
Zero is the product when either factor is 0; here both are 1.
questions.prompt: For binary `y₁ = 1`, `y₂ = 1`, the three And constraints give the interval of allowed `z`. What does this print?

sections.title: Linearizing products

units.summary: How the way you write a mixed-integer model decides whether the solver can solve it, and whether its answer is right: the LP relaxation bound and why a tighter formulation helps, sizing big-M from variable bounds, a big M that lets the integrality tolerance open a facility by a millionth, a small M that silently cuts off the optimum, indicator constraints and how HiGHS reformulates them, and linearizing products of binaries, all on a facility-location model with deterministic relaxation bounds.
units.title: Modelling discipline in JuMP: integer programs

hints: One loop over the indices, a running total that starts as a `Float64`, and the square of each difference. `eachindex(x, y)` checks the lengths for you.
The loop is a reduction, so the compiler keeps it in order unless you allow reordering: put `@simd` (with `@inbounds`) on it.
problems.prompt:
Write `sqdist(x, y)` for two `Vector{Float64}` that returns
`sum((x[i] - y[i])^2)` as a `Float64`, in one pass, without allocating, and
in a loop the compiler can vectorize. Vectors of different lengths must
throw a `DimensionMismatch`; empty vectors give `0.0`.

```julia
sqdist([1.0, 2.0, 3.0], [1.0, 0.0, 1.0])   # 8.0
sqdist(Float64[], Float64[])               # 0.0
sqdist([1.0], [1.0, 2.0])                  # DimensionMismatch
```

Results are compared with `rtol = 1e-12`: every term is non-negative, so
any order of summation has a relative error of at most about `(n + 2) u`,
`2.2e-13` for the largest case (`n = 2000`), and two orders agree to
twice that. Speed and allocations are graded against the reference on a
vector of 1000 elements, small enough to stay in the cache: there a loop
the compiler cannot vectorize is several times slower than one it can.
problems.title: A SIMD-friendly squared distance

hints: The starter counts serially and misses the `+ 1` (bins are 1-based). Fix the bin, then split the work: `Iterators.partition(eachindex(xs), len)` gives the chunks.
Inside each task, count into a vector the task created itself, and return it; after `fetch`ing every task, add the vectors.
problems.prompt:
Write `threaded_histogram(xs, nbins, ntasks)` for a `Vector{Float64}` `xs`
with values in `[0, 1)`, a positive `nbins` and a positive `ntasks`. Value
`x` falls in bin `min(floor(Int, x * nbins) + 1, nbins)`. Split the
indices of `xs` into at most `ntasks` contiguous chunks, count each chunk in
its own task (`Threads.@spawn`), and return the total counts as a
`Vector{Int}` of length `nbins`.

```julia
threaded_histogram([0.05, 0.15, 0.17, 0.95], 10, 2)   # [1, 2, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 1]
threaded_histogram(Float64[], 3, 4)                   # [0, 0, 0]
```

This problem is graded on **2 threads**, and every case runs 10 times. If
the tasks increment one shared counts vector, increments are lost and the
totals change from run to run: the grader reports that as a data race. Give
each task its own counts and add them at the end. Speed is graded against
the reference.
problems.starter:
function threaded_histogram(xs, nbins, ntasks)
    counts = zeros(Int, nbins)
    for x in xs
        counts[floor(Int, x * nbins)] += 1
    end
    return counts
end
problems.title: A race-free threaded histogram

hints: The starter returns Amdahl's number twice. Gustafson's formula uses the serial share of the parallel run: the serial part stays `s`, the parallel part was `p` times as much work.
For item 3, write down the job's time on one processor: the serial part `s` plus the parallel part done by one processor alone, `(1 - s) p`.
problems.prompt:
Write `speedup_models(s, p)` for a serial fraction `s` (a `Float64` in
`[0, 1]`) and a processor count `p` (an `Int`, at least 1). Return a
tuple of three `Float64`:

1. Amdahl's speedup on `p` processors when `s` is the serial fraction of
   the **one-processor** run time: `1 / (s + (1 - s) / p)`;
2. Gustafson's scaled speedup when `s` is the serial fraction of the
   **`p`-processor** run time: `s + (1 - s) p`;
3. the serial fraction that the job of item 2 has when run on **one**
   processor (its serial time divided by its one-processor time).

Throw an `ArgumentError` when `s` is outside `[0, 1]` or `p < 1`.

```julia
speedup_models(0.1, 4)    # (3.0769..., 3.7, 0.027027...)
speedup_models(0.0, 8)    # (8.0, 8.0, 0.0)
```

A check on your third number: Amdahl's formula with it as the serial
fraction gives Gustafson's speedup (item 2). Results are compared with
`rtol = 1e-12`: each item is a few operations, so different correct
formulas agree to a few roundings, about `1e-15` relative.
problems.title: Amdahl and Gustafson from a serial fraction

sections.body:
Unit 18 started threads and unit 14 made one core fast. This unit asks how
much faster several cores can make a numerical loop, and what stops them.
It relies on four facts:

* **`@simd` lets the compiler reorder a reduction** so it can use vector
  instructions, and arrays are column-major, so the first index should vary
  fastest (unit 14, section "Loops: memory order, hoisting, @inbounds and
  @simd").
* **Measure after a warm-up call and keep the minimum of several runs**;
  timings vary between runs and machines, so timing examples here are
  recorded, not checked (unit 14, section "Measuring without fooling
  yourself").
* **Tasks that update shared state race**; per-task partial results combined
  at the end avoid it (unit 18, sections "Concurrency is not parallelism:
  threads" and "Data races and how to avoid them").
* **Floating-point addition is not associative**, so a sum in another order
  has other last digits (unit 30, section "Every operation rounds, and the
  errors add up").

**How the examples get two threads.** The number of threads is fixed when
Julia starts, and this site runs each example in a Julia with one thread,
in a container allowed two CPUs' worth of time. That is a time quota, not
two cores reserved for it: the operating system may place the two threads on
two hyperthreads of one physical core, which share its caches and its
arithmetic units, and another program on the machine can take their time.
The examples that measure parallel speed write their code to a file and
start a second Julia with `--threads=2`, the same as running
`julia -t 2 file.jl` on your machine. `Base.julia_cmd()` passes no
`--project`, so that second Julia sees only the standard library; a script
that needs a package (say `using OhMyThreads`) must be started with
`--project=$(Base.active_project())` added. Every speedup in this unit is
measured on those two threads; nothing here is extrapolated to more cores
except by a model that says so.
sections.title: What you need from earlier units

sections.body:
A modern core does not add one pair of numbers per instruction. Its vector
(SIMD, "single instruction, multiple data") registers hold several numbers,
four `Float64` in a 256-bit AVX2 register and eight with AVX-512, and one
instruction adds them all. A loop runs on these registers only when the
compiler can prove the result does not change, or is told it may change:

* `a[i] = b[i] + c[i]` has independent iterations, so the compiler
  vectorizes it without help (the bounds checks inside the loop can prevent
  it; `eachindex` or `@inbounds` removes them).
* `s += x[i]` is a chain: each addition needs the previous `s`. Four lanes
  would compute four partial sums and add them at the end, which is a
  different order of additions and so a different rounding. The compiler may
  not change your floating-point results on its own, so it keeps the chain;
  `@simd` grants permission to reassociate.

Vector loads read **contiguous** memory. This is where the layout of the
data matters. An array of structs (AoS), `Vector{Particle}` with fields
`x, y, z, m`, stores the four fields of each particle next to each other, so
the `x` values are 32 bytes apart. A loop over all `x` loads a cache line of
64 bytes to use 16 of them, and the compiler has to gather scattered values
into a register. A struct of arrays (SoA), one `Vector{Float64}` per field,
puts the `x` values side by side: every byte loaded is used, and loads are
plain vector loads. Which layout is better depends on the access pattern: a
loop that uses all four fields of each particle reads AoS contiguously too.

examples.caption: The layout of an array of structs: `Particle` is 32 bytes with `x` at offset 0, so consecutive `x` values are 32 bytes apart in memory. The SoA copy holds the same numbers contiguously.
examples.code:
using Random
struct Particle
    x::Float64
    y::Float64
    z::Float64
    m::Float64
end
rng = Xoshiro(1)
aos = [Particle(rand(rng), rand(rng), rand(rng), 1.0) for _ in 1:1000]
xs = [p.x for p in aos]                       # struct of arrays: the x field alone
println("sizeof(Particle) = ", sizeof(Particle), " bytes; offset of y = ", fieldoffset(Particle, 2))
println("stride of x in the AoS: ", sizeof(Particle) ÷ sizeof(Float64), " Float64")
function sumx(ps::Vector{Particle})
    s = 0.0
    @inbounds @simd for i in eachindex(ps)
        s += ps[i].x
    end
    return s
end
function sumx(x::Vector{Float64})
    s = 0.0
    @inbounds @simd for i in eachindex(x)
        s += x[i]
    end
    return s
end
println("same sum to rounding: ", isapprox(sumx(aos), sumx(xs); rtol = 1000 * eps()))
examples.notice: Notice that both layouts sum to the same value (to rounding: `@simd` reorders the sum differently for the two loops), and that the AoS stride is four `Float64`.
examples.output:
sizeof(Particle) = 32 bytes; offset of y = 8
stride of x in the AoS: 4 Float64
same sum to rounding: true

examples.caption: Time per sum: a plain loop and the `@simd` loop on 4096 `Float64` (32 KB, which stays in the cache), then on 4 million (32 MB, read from memory) together with `sum` of the SoA field and the `@simd` sum of the AoS field. Recorded, not checked: timings vary between runs and CPUs.
examples.code:
using Random
struct Particle
    x::Float64
    y::Float64
    z::Float64
    m::Float64
end
function plain_sum(x)
    s = 0.0
    for i in eachindex(x)
        s += x[i]
    end
    return s
end
function simd_sum(x)
    s = 0.0
    @inbounds @simd for i in eachindex(x)
        s += x[i]
    end
    return s
end
function simd_sumx(ps)
    s = 0.0
    @inbounds @simd for i in eachindex(ps)
        s += ps[i].x
    end
    return s
end
const sink = Ref(0.0)                      # results are used, so the compiler cannot drop the calls
function per_call(f, x, reps)              # best of 10 rounds of `reps` calls, in seconds per call
    sink[] += f(x)
    return minimum(@elapsed(for _ in 1:reps; sink[] += f(x); end) for _ in 1:10) / reps
end
rng = Xoshiro(1)
small = rand(rng, 2^12)
println("4096 elements (cached):  plain loop ", round(per_call(plain_sum, small, 1000) * 1e6; digits = 2),
        " µs,  @simd ", round(per_call(simd_sum, small, 1000) * 1e6; digits = 2), " µs")
n = 2^22
aos = [Particle(rand(rng), rand(rng), rand(rng), 1.0) for _ in 1:n]
xs = [p.x for p in aos]
for (name, f, x) in (("plain loop, SoA", plain_sum, xs), ("@simd, SoA     ", simd_sum, xs),
                     ("sum, SoA       ", sum, xs), ("@simd, AoS     ", simd_sumx, aos))
    println("4M elements, ", name, "  ", round(per_call(f, x, 1) * 1e3; digits = 2), " ms")
end
examples.notice: Notice what each pair compares. On the cached vector nothing waits for memory, so the plain loop is held back only by its chain of additions, and that is where `@simd` should gain most (several times on a quiet machine). On the 32 MB vector both loops also wait for memory, which shrinks the gap (the next section explains why). The AoS loop loads four times the memory for the same additions, so it should be the slowest. A busy machine adds noise to all of these numbers; rerun to compare.
examples.output:
4096 elements (cached):  plain loop 4.38 µs,  @simd 0.28 µs
4M elements, plain loop, SoA  25.42 ms
4M elements, @simd, SoA       2.3 ms
4M elements, sum, SoA         5.36 ms
4M elements, @simd, AoS       21.02 ms

choices: Splitting the sum into lanes changes its rounding, which needs permission
Vector registers cannot hold `Float64` values
The bounds checks on `x[i]` stay in the loop and block the vector instructions
questions.explain: Four lanes compute four partial sums and add them at the end: a different order of additions, so different last digits (floating-point addition is not associative). The compiler preserves your results unless `@simd` (or `@fastmath`) allows reassociation. `eachindex` already lets it drop the bounds checks.
misconceptions: AVX2 registers hold four `Float64` and AVX-512 eight; the `a[i] = b[i] + c[i]` loop is vectorized with them without any annotation.
`eachindex(x)` produces only valid indices, so the compiler removes the checks by itself; what remains is the dependency of each `s` on the previous one.
questions.prompt: Without `@simd`, why does the compiler not vectorize `for i in eachindex(x); s += x[i]; end` for a `Vector{Float64}`?

choices: Nothing for speed, since both layouts hold the same numbers in the same cache
It makes the loop safe to run on several threads
It reads one eighth of the memory, in contiguous vector loads
It removes the need for `@simd` on the reduction
questions.explain: In the AoS, consecutive `x` values are 64 bytes apart, so every cache line loaded carries one useful number. In the SoA each line carries eight `x` values, and the vector unit loads them in one instruction. The reduction still needs `@simd` to be reordered.
misconceptions: The numbers are the same, but the memory traffic is not: the loop moves whole cache lines, and in the AoS seven eighths of each line is fields it does not use.
Reading is race-free in either layout; layout changes speed, not thread safety.
Contiguous data makes vector loads possible, but reordering the sum still changes its rounding, so the compiler still needs `@simd`'s permission.
questions.prompt: A simulation stores particles as a `Vector{Particle}` with 8 `Float64` fields, and its hot loop reads only the `x` field of every particle. What does switching to one vector per field (struct of arrays) change for that loop?

sections.title: SIMD and data layout

sections.body:
A core can do arithmetic much faster than memory can deliver operands. So
each loop has two possible limits, and the lower one wins. The **roofline
model** ([Williams, Waterman and Patterson 2009](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roofline_model))
states it as

    attainable FLOP/s = min(peak FLOP/s,  I × bandwidth)

where the **arithmetic intensity** `I` is the number of floating-point
operations per byte moved between memory and the core. Two kernels on
arrays too large for the caches:

* **The stream triad** `a[i] = b[i] + s * c[i]` does 2 flops and asks for
  24 bytes (read `b[i]` and `c[i]`, write `a[i]`): `I = 1/12` flop per byte.
  At a bandwidth of 10 GB/s it cannot exceed about 0.8 GFLOP/s, a small
  fraction of what one core can compute. It is **bandwidth-bound**. (Most
  caches read a line before writing into it, "write-allocate", so the
  hardware moves 32 bytes per element; a GB/s figure computed from 24 bytes
  is a quarter lower than the real traffic.)
* **A degree-64 polynomial** evaluated by Horner's rule at each `b[i]` does
  128 flops (64 multiply-adds) and moves 16 bytes: `I = 8`. Memory is not
  its limit; the core is. Here it is not even the core's peak: each
  multiply-add needs the previous one's result, the same chain as
  `s += x[i]` in the first section, so the loop runs at one multiply-add per
  latency of that instruction, a small fraction of the peak. It is
  **latency-bound**, which for threads behaves like compute-bound: each core
  runs its own chains.

What this predicts for threads: a second core doubles the arithmetic but
not the memory bandwidth, which the cores share. A kernel limited inside the
core can nearly double its speed on two threads; a bandwidth-bound one gains
only as much as one core was failing to use of the memory system. One core
often draws a large share of the bandwidth on its own, so the triad's
speedup is below 2 by an amount that depends on the machine, which is why
the example measures it instead of asserting it.

examples.caption: Arithmetic intensity of the two kernels from their flop and byte counts, and the bandwidth-bound ceiling each would have at an assumed 10 GB/s (the assumption is only for the arithmetic).
examples.code:
kernels = (("triad    a[i] = b[i] + s*c[i]", 2, 3 * 8), ("Horner-64 a[i] = p(b[i])  ", 128, 2 * 8))
for (name, flops, bytes) in kernels
    I = flops / bytes
    println(name, "  I = ", rpad(round(I; digits = 3), 6), " flop/byte,  ceiling at 10 GB/s: ",
            round(I * 10; digits = 2), " GFLOP/s")
end
examples.notice: Notice the factor of 96 between the intensities: the triad's ceiling at 10 GB/s is below 1 GFLOP/s, while the polynomial's is 80 GFLOP/s, more than a chain of dependent multiply-adds can reach, so its limit is in the core.
examples.output:
triad    a[i] = b[i] + s*c[i]  I = 0.083  flop/byte,  ceiling at 10 GB/s: 0.83 GFLOP/s
Horner-64 a[i] = p(b[i])    I = 8.0    flop/byte,  ceiling at 10 GB/s: 80.0 GFLOP/s

examples.caption: The triad on 8 million elements and the polynomial on 1 million, timed with 1 and 2 tasks in a Julia started with 2 threads. Recorded, not checked: the numbers depend on the CPU, its memory and what else the machine is running.
examples.code:
write("roofline.jl", raw"""
using Base.Threads
function triad!(a, b, c, s, r)
    @inbounds @simd for i in r
        a[i] = b[i] + s * c[i]
    end
end
function horner!(a, b, r)
    @inbounds for i in r
        x = b[i]
        y = 0.0
        for k in 1:64
            y = muladd(y, x, 1.0)
        end
        a[i] = y
    end
end
function on_tasks(f, ntasks, n)            # ntasks contiguous chunks, one task each
    @sync for r in Iterators.partition(1:n, cld(n, ntasks))
        @spawn f(r)
    end
end
best(f) = (f(); minimum(@elapsed(f()) for _ in 1:5))
n, m = 2^23, 2^20                         # triad on 8M elements (far beyond the caches), Horner on 1M
a, b, c = zeros(n), rand(n), rand(n)
println("threads: ", nthreads())
for (name, k, flops, bytes, len) in (("triad ", r -> triad!(a, b, c, 3.0, r), 2, 24, n),
                                     ("Horner", r -> horner!(a, b, r), 128, 16, m))
    t1 = best(() -> on_tasks(k, 1, len))
    t2 = best(() -> on_tasks(k, 2, len))
    println(name, "  1 thread: ", round(bytes * len / t1 / 1e9; digits = 1), " GB/s, ",
            round(flops * len / t1 / 1e9; digits = 1), " GFLOP/s;  speedup on 2 threads: ", round(t1 / t2; digits = 2))
end
""")
run(`$(Base.julia_cmd()) --threads=2 roofline.jl`);
examples.notice: Notice the triad's GB/s (counted at 24 bytes per element, so a quarter below the real traffic): it is the memory system's speed, and the model predicts a speedup below 2 for it, by a machine-dependent amount. For the polynomial it predicts close to 2 on two real cores, since each computes its half independently. Two hyperthreads of one core share its arithmetic, and a busy machine takes time and bandwidth from both kernels, so a measurement can fall short of either prediction; rerun to compare.
examples.output:
threads: 2
triad   1 thread: 17.4 GB/s, 1.5 GFLOP/s;  speedup on 2 threads: 1.44
Horner  1 thread: 0.6 GB/s, 4.7 GFLOP/s;  speedup on 2 threads: 2.02

choices: A speedup near 2, since the iterations are independent and split evenly in two
A speedup bounded by how much more memory bandwidth two cores get
No change at all, since threads cannot share one array
questions.explain: Axpy does 2 flops per 24 bytes (read `x[i]` and `y[i]`, write `y[i]`), `I = 1/12`: bandwidth-bound. Two cores share the memory bus, so the speedup is the ratio of the bandwidth two cores draw to what one draws, often well under 2 and machine-dependent.
misconceptions: Independent iterations make the loop safe to split, but both halves still wait on the same memory system; the arithmetic was never the limit.
Threads share memory, and splitting the index range between them is race-free; the gain is small because memory is the limit, not because sharing fails.
questions.prompt: A kernel computes `y[i] = a * x[i] + y[i]` (axpy) on vectors of 100 million `Float64`. On two threads instead of one, what does the roofline model predict?

sections.title: Memory bandwidth and the roofline

sections.body:
Julia offers three levels for splitting a loop over threads:

* **`Threads.@threads for ...`** splits the iteration range into one chunk
  per thread. Good for a loop whose iterations write to separate places.
* **`Threads.@spawn`** starts one task per piece of work, which the
  scheduler places on any thread; you choose the chunks and combine the
  results yourself (unit 18).
* **OhMyThreads.jl** packages the per-chunk pattern: `tmap(f, xs)` and
  `tmapreduce(f, op, xs)` split `xs` into contiguous chunks, one task each
  (by default as many as threads), reduce each chunk, then combine the
  partial results in order. Its documentation requires `op` to be
  associative and says that "each chunk consists of contiguous elements and
  order is maintained" ([OhMyThreads API](https://juliafolds2.github.io/OhMyThreads.jl/stable/refs/api/)).

One pattern looks race-free and still runs slowly: per-thread accumulators
in neighbouring slots of one array, `acc[t] += x[i]`. No two tasks write
the same element, so the result is right. But caches move memory in lines
of typically 64 bytes, and when one core writes its slot, the line holding
the other core's slot is invalidated too, so the two cores pass the line
back and forth on every write. That is **false sharing**
([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/False_sharing)). Padding the
slots apart removes it: 128 bytes rather than 64, because many CPUs also
fetch the neighbouring line of each line they load, so two adjacent lines
can still interfere. A local variable per task, returned at the end,
removes the shared array altogether.

A pattern from older code is unsafe: indexing buffers by
`Threads.threadid()`. The Julia manual says `threadid()` "should not be
treated as constant within a task" and "Buffers should not be managed
based on `threadid()`" ([multi-threading manual](https://docs.julialang.org/en/v1.10/manual/multi-threading/)):
a task can move to another thread, and two tasks on one thread can share the
buffer.

examples.caption: `tmapreduce` with 1, 2 and 4 tasks against a serial `mapreduce` (on this site's single thread the tasks take turns, but the chunking is the same as on many threads).
examples.code:
using OhMyThreads, Random
x = randn(Xoshiro(3), 10^6)
serial = mapreduce(abs2, +, x)
for nt in (1, 2, 4)
    r = tmapreduce(abs2, +, x; ntasks = nt)
    println("ntasks = ", nt, ": ", round(r; sigdigits = 12), "   ≈ serial (rtol 1e-14): ", isapprox(r, serial; rtol = 1e-14))
end
examples.notice: Notice that the threaded results agree with the serial one to a relative `1e-14`. They are printed to 12 digits because the last digits are not fixed: each number of tasks adds the terms in another order, each chunk is summed with SIMD instructions whose width depends on the CPU, and the next section shows chunkings whose last digits differ.
examples.output:
ntasks = 1: 999655.955579   ≈ serial (rtol 1e-14): true
ntasks = 2: 999655.955579   ≈ serial (rtol 1e-14): true
ntasks = 4: 999655.955579   ≈ serial (rtol 1e-14): true

examples.caption: False sharing on 2 threads: each task adds its half of a small vector, 1000 times over, into its own slot of a shared array, with the two slots adjacent (one cache line) or 128 bytes apart, against a local variable per task. Recorded, not checked: timings vary between runs and CPUs.
examples.code:
write("false_sharing.jl", raw"""
using Base.Threads
function slot_sum(x, stride, reps)          # task t accumulates into acc[(t - 1) * stride + 1]
    acc = zeros(2 * stride)
    h = length(x) ÷ 2
    @sync for t in 1:2
        @spawn begin
            j = (t - 1) * stride + 1
            for _ in 1:reps, i in (t - 1) * h + 1:t * h
                @inbounds acc[j] += x[i]
            end
        end
    end
    return acc[1] + acc[stride + 1]
end
function local_sum(x, reps)
    h = length(x) ÷ 2
    tasks = [@spawn begin
                 s = 0.0
                 for _ in 1:reps, i in (t - 1) * h + 1:t * h
                     @inbounds s += x[i]
                 end
                 s
             end for t in 1:2]
    return fetch(tasks[1]) + fetch(tasks[2])
end
x = rand(2^14)                              # 128 KB: stays in cache, so memory speed does not hide the effect
best(f) = (f(); minimum(@elapsed(f()) for _ in 1:5))
println("threads: ", nthreads(), "; same sums: ", slot_sum(x, 1, 2) == slot_sum(x, 16, 2) == local_sum(x, 2))
println("adjacent slots (one cache line): ", round(best(() -> slot_sum(x, 1, 1000)) * 1e3; digits = 1), " ms")
println("slots 128 bytes apart:           ", round(best(() -> slot_sum(x, 16, 1000)) * 1e3; digits = 1), " ms")
println("a local variable per task:       ", round(best(() -> local_sum(x, 1000)) * 1e3; digits = 1), " ms")
""")
run(`$(Base.julia_cmd()) --threads=2 false_sharing.jl`);
examples.notice: Notice that all three give the same sum. On two separate cores the adjacent slots should be the slowest, since every write by one core takes the cache line away from the other; padding should help, and the local variable should be fastest because it never touches shared memory inside the loop. If the two threads land on hyperthreads of one core, they share its cache and the effect can vanish; a machine busy with other work can swamp it too. Rerun to compare.
examples.output:
threads: 2; same sums: true
adjacent slots (one cache line): 8.9 ms
slots 128 bytes apart:           8.8 ms
a local variable per task:       8.9 ms

choices: The two tasks write the same element, so updates are lost
`Vector{Float64}` is not thread-safe, so Julia takes a lock around each element write
Both slots sit on one cache line, which the cores keep taking from each other
questions.explain: Each task writes only its own element, so there is no race. But the two elements are 8 bytes apart, inside one 64-byte cache line, and a write by one core invalidates that line in the other core's cache. Padding the slots apart or keeping the sum in a local variable fixes it.
misconceptions: Lost updates would make the result wrong; here each task owns one element. The cost is in the hardware's cache coherence, not in the program's logic.
Julia adds no locks to array writes; arrays are not thread-safe, which is why races are the programmer's job. The slowdown comes from the cache line both slots live on.
questions.prompt: Two tasks each sum half of a vector into `acc[1]` and `acc[2]` of a shared `Vector{Float64}`. The result is correct but slower than on one thread. Why?

sections.title: Threads in practice: OhMyThreads and false sharing

sections.body:
A parallel reduction with `p` chunks computes `p` partial sums and then adds
them. That is a different parenthesization of the same sum, so by unit 30's
rule it rounds differently. Three consequences:

* **The result depends on the number of chunks.** With OhMyThreads' default
  of one chunk per thread, the same program gives different last digits on 2
  and on 8 threads. For a fixed number of chunks the result is repeatable,
  because the partial sums are combined in chunk order.
* **None of the answers is "the" right one.** Each is a different rounding
  of the true sum, and all obey the same bound: the error of summing `n`
  terms in any order is at most about `(n - 1) u` times `sum(abs, x)`, with
  `u = eps() / 2`. With `p` chunks the worst-case bound shrinks to about
  `(n/p + p - 2) u sum(abs, x)`, since each term passes through a shorter
  chain of additions. That is a bound, not a prediction: random rounding
  errors mostly cancel, and in the example below the measured errors do not
  shrink steadily as the chunks get more numerous.
* **Tests must compare with a tolerance**, derived from that bound, never
  with `==` against a serial run. The tolerance is relative to
  `sum(abs, x)`, not to the sum: with cancellation the sum can be much
  smaller than the terms.

The example below uses a plain loop for each chunk, so its digits depend
only on the chunking and are the same on every machine.

examples.caption: One million `randn` terms summed with 1, 2, 3, 4 and 8 contiguous chunks (a plain loop per chunk, partial sums added in order), against the exact sum computed in `BigFloat`.
examples.code:
using Random
x = randn(Xoshiro(7), 10^6)
function chunked_sum(x, nchunks)
    total = 0.0
    for r in Iterators.partition(eachindex(x), cld(length(x), nchunks))
        s = 0.0
        for i in r
            s += x[i]
        end
        total += s
    end
    return total
end
exact = sum(big.(x))
bound = (length(x) - 1) * eps() / 2 * sum(abs, x)
println("bound on the error: ", round(bound; sigdigits = 2))
for nc in (1, 2, 3, 4, 8)
    s = chunked_sum(x, nc)
    println(rpad(nc, 2), "chunks: ", rpad(s, 22), " error ", rpad(round(Float64(abs(s - exact)); sigdigits = 2), 9),
            " within bound: ", abs(s - exact) <= bound)
end
examples.notice: Notice that the five chunkings give different floats, every one of them within the bound `(n - 1) u sum(abs, x)`, and that the error is far below the bound (rounding errors of random sign mostly cancel).
examples.output:
bound on the error: 8.9e-5
1 chunks: 293.1599232981022      error 2.3e-11   within bound: true
2 chunks: 293.1599232981044      error 2.5e-11   within bound: true
3 chunks: 293.159923298084       error 4.9e-12   within bound: true
4 chunks: 293.1599232981043      error 2.5e-11   within bound: true
8 chunks: 293.1599232980958      error 1.7e-11   within bound: true

questions.explain: In one chunk, `1.0 + 1e-16` rounds to `1.0` (below half the spacing `eps() = 2.2e-16`), twice, and `-1.0` cancels it to `0.0`. In two chunks the second chunk is `1e-16 - 1.0`, which rounds to `-prevfloat(1.0) = -(1 - 1.1e-16)`; adding it to `1.0` gives `1.1e-16`. The true sum is `2e-16`, and neither order gets it.
misconceptions: The second chunk does not round the same way: `1e-16 - 1.0` lands next to `-1.0`, where floats are spaced `1.1e-16` apart, so it rounds to `-(1 - 1.1e-16)`, not to `-1.0`.
That is the exact sum; both orders lose digits to rounding against the large terms, and they lose different digits.
The orders are swapped: the single chain rounds both small terms away against `1.0` before the cancellation.
questions.prompt: Four numbers summed in one chunk and in two. What does this print?

choices: `==`, since both add the same numbers
`isapprox` with `rtol = eps()`
`abs(a - b) <= 2(n - 1) * (eps() / 2) * sum(abs, x)`
Compare only the first 8 printed digits, since the rest is rounding noise
questions.explain: Each order's error is at most `(n - 1) u sum(abs, x)`, so two orders differ by at most twice that. The bound is relative to `sum(abs, x)`, which matters when terms cancel: then the sum is small and a relative tolerance on it is far too tight.
misconceptions: The same numbers in a different order round differently; `==` fails as soon as the chunking changes, for example on a machine with more threads.
One `eps` is the error of a single operation; a million additions can each contribute one, and with cancellation the sum is small compared with the terms.
A fixed number of digits ignores cancellation: if the terms nearly cancel, the first 8 digits of the sum may already be rounding noise, and the check fails on a correct program.
questions.prompt: A test checks a threaded `tmapreduce(+, ...)` sum of a million terms against a serial loop. Which check is right?

sections.title: Why a threaded sum changes its last digits

sections.body:
**Amdahl's law** ([Amdahl 1967](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amdahl%27s_law))
asks: for a **fixed problem**, how much faster is it on `p` processors? If a
fraction `f` of the one-processor run time parallelizes perfectly and the
rest `1 - f` does not,

    S_A(p) = 1 / ((1 - f) + f / p),     S_A(∞) = 1 / (1 - f)

A program that is 90% parallel never runs more than 10 times faster, on any
number of cores. The serial part includes everything that does not split:
setup, I/O, a reduction's final combine, the time to start tasks.

**Gustafson's law** ([Gustafson 1988](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustafson%27s_law))
asks another question: with `p` processors, **how much more work** can you
do in the same time? Here `s` is the serial fraction of the run time
measured **on the `p`-processor run**, and the scaled speedup is

    S_G(p) = s + (1 - s) p

It grows without limit, because the parallel part is assumed to grow with
`p` (a finer grid, more samples) while the serial part stays the same.

The two laws do not contradict each other: they describe different
experiments, and their `s` are measured differently. A job with serial
fraction `s` on `p` processors had serial fraction
`s / (s + (1 - s) p)` when run on one; put that into Amdahl's formula and it
gives Gustafson's number. Use Amdahl when the problem size is fixed (a
given simulation, faster) and Gustafson when the time budget is fixed (a
bigger simulation, in the same time).

The models also say how to read a measurement. A measured speedup `S` on
`p` threads implies an effective serial fraction
`e = (1/S - 1/p) / (1 - 1/p)`, Amdahl's formula solved for the serial
fraction, known as the **Karp-Flatt metric**
([Karp and Flatt 1990](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karp%E2%80%93Flatt_metric)). If `e` grows with
`p`, the loss is not a fixed serial part but an overhead that grows with
the threads, such as shared memory bandwidth.

examples.caption: Amdahl's speedup for three parallel fractions, and Gustafson's for the same numbers read as serial shares of the parallel run.
examples.code:
amdahl(f, p) = 1 / ((1 - f) + f / p)
gustafson(s, p) = s + (1 - s) * p
println("parallel fraction f   p = 2    p = 8    p = 64   p = ∞")
for f in (0.5, 0.9, 0.99)
    println(rpad(f, 22), join((rpad(round(amdahl(f, p); digits = 2), 9) for p in (2, 8, 64)), ""),
            round(1 / (1 - f); digits = 1))
end
println("serial share s (Gustafson)")
for s in (0.5, 0.1, 0.01)
    println(rpad(s, 22), join((rpad(round(gustafson(s, p); digits = 2), 9) for p in (2, 8, 64)), ""), "∞")
end
println("Amdahl with s converted to one processor equals Gustafson: ",
        all(amdahl(1 - s / (s + (1 - s) * p), p) ≈ gustafson(s, p) for s in (0.5, 0.1, 0.01), p in (2, 8, 64)))
examples.notice: Notice the ceilings in the last column: a 99%-parallel program is capped at 100x. Gustafson's numbers grow linearly with `p` instead, because they answer a different question (more work in the same time).
examples.output:
parallel fraction f   p = 2    p = 8    p = 64   p = ∞
0.5                   1.33     1.78     1.97     2.0
0.9                   1.82     4.71     8.77     10.0
0.99                  1.98     7.48     39.26    100.0
serial share s (Gustafson)
0.5                   1.5      4.5      32.5     ∞
0.1                   1.9      7.3      57.7     ∞
0.01                  1.99     7.93     63.37    ∞
Amdahl with s converted to one processor equals Gustafson: true

examples.caption: A program with a serial part (a recurrence, each step of which needs the previous one) and a parallel part (the Horner kernel): Amdahl's prediction for 2 threads from the measured one-thread fraction, against the measured speedup. Recorded, not checked: timings vary.
examples.code:
write("amdahl.jl", raw"""
using Base.Threads, Random
function horner!(a, b, r)
    @inbounds for i in r
        x = b[i]
        y = 0.0
        for k in 1:64
            y = muladd(y, x, 1.0)
        end
        a[i] = y
    end
end
function logistic(x, m)                                   # each step needs the previous one: serial
    for _ in 1:m
        x = 3.7 * x * (1 - x)
    end
    return x
end
function job(b, a, ntasks)
    x = logistic(0.3, 5_000_000)                          # the serial stage
    @sync for r in Iterators.partition(eachindex(b), cld(length(b), ntasks))
        @spawn horner!(a, b, r)                           # the parallel stage
    end
    return x
end
n = 2^20
a, b = zeros(n), rand(Xoshiro(1), n)
const sink = Ref(0.0)                                     # results are used, so no call is optimized away
best(f) = (f(); minimum(@elapsed(sink[] += f()) for _ in 1:5))
t_serial = best(() -> logistic(0.3, 5_000_000))
t1 = best(() -> job(b, a, 1))
t2 = best(() -> job(b, a, 2))
f = 1 - t_serial / t1
S = t1 / t2
amdahl(f, p) = 1 / ((1 - f) + f / p)
println("threads: ", nthreads(), "; measured parallel fraction f = ", round(f; digits = 3))
println("Amdahl predicts S(2) = ", round(amdahl(f, 2); digits = 2), "; measured S(2) = ", round(S; digits = 2))
println("serial fraction implied by S(2): ", round((1 / S - 1 / 2) / (1 - 1 / 2); digits = 3),
        "; measured directly: ", round(1 - f; digits = 3))
println("model only, not measured: S(8) = ", round(amdahl(f, 8); digits = 1), ", S(∞) = ", round(1 / (1 - f); digits = 1))
""")
run(`$(Base.julia_cmd()) --threads=2 amdahl.jl`);
examples.notice: Notice how the prediction from `f` compares with the measured speedup, and the serial fraction implied by the measurement (the Karp-Flatt metric) with the one measured directly. Where they differ, the gap is the overhead Amdahl's model leaves out: starting tasks, shared caches, hyperthreads, or other programs taking the CPU. Anything beyond 2 threads in the last line is the model, not a measurement.
examples.output:
threads: 2; measured parallel fraction f = 0.699
Amdahl predicts S(2) = 1.54; measured S(2) = 1.44
serial fraction implied by S(2): 0.391; measured directly: 0.301
model only, not measured: S(8) = 2.6, S(∞) = 3.3

choices: At most 20 on any number of cores, and about 15 on 64
About 64, since 95% of the work is parallel
About 61, from Gustafson's scaled speedup `s + (1 - s) p` with `s = 0.05`
questions.explain: `S = 1 / (0.05 + 0.95/64) ≈ 15.4`, and no number of cores passes `1/0.05 = 20`: the serial 5% alone takes 1/20 of the original time. Gustafson's 61 answers how much **bigger** a problem 64 cores can do in the same time, which is not this question.
misconceptions: The serial 5% runs at one core's speed however many cores there are; it alone takes 1/20 of the original time.
Gustafson's formula assumes the parallel work grows with the cores; for a fixed problem the serial part is a growing share of the run, and Amdahl's law applies.
questions.prompt: A fixed-size simulation spends 5% of its one-core run time in serial setup. Its author buys a 64-core machine. What does Amdahl's law say about the speedup?

sections.body:
Unit 18's section "Beyond one process: Distributed and GPUs" introduced
worker **processes**: `addprocs`, `@everywhere` and `pmap` from the
Distributed standard library. One more call is used here:
`remotecall_fetch(f, id, args...)` runs `f` on worker `id` and returns the
result ([Distributed manual](https://docs.julialang.org/en/v1.10/stdlib/Distributed/)).
Each worker has its own memory, so arguments are **copied** to it and
results copied back: a worker that mutates an argument mutates its copy.
That costs time per call, so processes pay off for large independent jobs
(a parameter sweep, an ensemble of long simulations), and they are the only
way to use more than one machine. Starting a worker is a new Julia process,
which takes seconds; the example starts one on this machine.

**GPUs** run one small function, a **kernel**, for every index of a range,
in groups of threads (workgroups) that share fast memory. The kernel sees
only its own index and must not depend on the order in which indices run.
KernelAbstractions.jl writes such kernels once and runs them on several
backends: `@kernel` defines it, `@index(Global)` gives the work item's
index, and `kernel(backend, workgroupsize)(args...; ndrange = n)` launches
it ([KernelAbstractions quickstart](https://juliagpu.github.io/KernelAbstractions.jl/v0.9/quickstart/)).
The `CPU()` backend runs the same kernel on the CPU's threads, so a kernel
can be written and tested without a GPU; CUDA.jl, AMDGPU.jl and Metal.jl
provide the GPU backends (not installed here). The roofline applies to GPUs
too: they have far more arithmetic and more bandwidth than a CPU, and a
bandwidth-bound kernel is still bandwidth-bound there.

examples.caption: One worker process: its id, a `pmap` over it, and what happens when a worker mutates an argument.
examples.code:
using Distributed
ENV["JULIA_WORKER_TIMEOUT"] = "200"            # seconds a new worker waits to connect (default 60), for busy machines
println("new workers: ", addprocs(1))
@everywhere square_where(x) = (x^2, myid())
println(pmap(square_where, 1:4))
v = [1, 2, 3]
w = remotecall_fetch(u -> (u[1] = 100; u), 2, v)
println("worker's copy: ", w, "   this process: ", v)
rmprocs(workers());
examples.notice: Notice that every element of the `pmap` ran on worker 2, and that the vector `v` in this process is unchanged after the worker set its first element to 100: the worker received a copy.

examples.caption: The stream triad as a KernelAbstractions kernel on the `CPU()` backend, checked against the broadcast `b .+ s .* c`.
examples.code:
using KernelAbstractions, Random
@kernel function triad_kernel!(a, @Const(b), @Const(c), s)
    i = @index(Global)
    @inbounds a[i] = b[i] + s * c[i]
end
n = 10^6
b, c = rand(Xoshiro(1), n), rand(Xoshiro(2), n)
a = similar(b)
backend = get_backend(a)                      # CPU() for an ordinary Array
triad_kernel!(backend, 256)(a, b, c, 3.0; ndrange = n)
KernelAbstractions.synchronize(backend)
println("backend: ", typeof(backend), "; equals the broadcast: ", a == b .+ 3.0 .* c)
examples.notice: Notice that the kernel's result equals the broadcast exactly: each work item computes `b[i] + s * c[i]` with the same two roundings, and no reduction is involved, so the order of indices cannot change any digit.
examples.output: backend: CPU; equals the broadcast: true

choices: It is doubled, since the worker shares the caller's memory
Julia raises an error, since arguments sent to workers are read-only
Nothing; the worker doubled its own copy of `A`, which stays there
questions.explain: Workers are separate processes: `A` is serialized, sent, and rebuilt in the worker's memory. The worker's `A .*= 2` changes that copy; return the result to get it back. Sending a large matrix each call also costs time, which is why processes suit large, independent jobs.
misconceptions: Threads share memory; processes do not. Distributed copies the argument to the worker.
Nothing makes the copy read-only; the worker mutates it freely, and the change stays on the worker.
questions.prompt: A function called on a worker with `remotecall_fetch(f, 2, A)` does `A .*= 2` on a large matrix `A`. What happens to `A` in the calling process?

choices: Work items run concurrently in no fixed order, so the updates race
Kernels may read their array arguments but never write to any of them
`@index(Global)` gives each work item the same index
questions.explain: A kernel is a function of one index, run for all indices concurrently in groups. Every work item doing a read-modify-write on `total[1]` is the data race of unit 18, on thousands of threads. Reductions on GPUs are written as per-group partial sums combined in a second step, or with atomics.
misconceptions: The triad kernel writes `a[i]`; writes are fine as long as each work item writes its own element.
Each work item gets its own index, which is what makes `a[i] = ...` race-free; the problem is many items writing one element.
questions.prompt: Why may a KernelAbstractions kernel not accumulate into one shared scalar with `total[1] += x[i]`?
